title: Concrete-hash security for restricted numerical circuit families
subfield: Fiat–Shamir and concrete-hash foundations
open: Can we find a concrete, checkable family of quantized inference circuits for which concrete-hash Fiat–Shamir GKR is adaptively sound? The target is a family with size \(S\le10^{12}\) and depth \(D\le10^4\), accompanied by an explicit 128-bit security analysis and an account of which compiler rewrites preserve the guarantee.
status: Khovratovich, Rothblum and Soukhanov’s 2025 attack covers selected GKR circuits, including functionally equivalent rewrites, but it does not establish that every fixed AI circuit is insecure (see [*How to Prove False Statements: Practical Attacks on Fiat-Shamir*, ePrint 2025/118](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/118)).
solved_when: A checkable family of quantized inference circuits with \(S\le10^{12}\) and \(D\le10^4\) is identified, together with an explicit 128-bit security analysis of adaptive soundness for concrete-hash Fiat–Shamir GKR on that family, and a specification of which compiler rewrites preserve the guarantee.
why: Security can depend on the circuit’s implementation, so mathematical equivalence alone is insufficient; without such a family, concrete-hash Fiat–Shamir GKR cannot be safely deployed for AI inference.
key_works: Dmitry Khovratovich, Ron D. Rothblum, Lev Soukhanov (2025), [*How to Prove False Statements: Practical Attacks on Fiat-Shamir*, ePrint 2025/118](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/118).

title: Standard-model succinct proofs for expressive hidden-model inference
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Can we build adaptively sound, publicly verifiable SNARGs for an explicitly NP-hard family of quantized inference statements, starting only from falsifiable standard-model assumptions via a non-black-box reduction? Concretely, the target is proof and verification complexity polynomial in \(\lambda\) and \(\log T\), or else a sharply scoped barrier showing this cannot be done.
status: The Gentry–Wichs result (2011, ePrint 2010/610) establishes a broad barrier for black-box reductions separating succinct non-interactive arguments from all falsifiable assumptions. Positive restricted-language constructions exist — e.g., Mathialagan et al. (2024, adaptively sound zero-knowledge SNARKs for UP, ePrint 2024/227) — but these do not resolve general expressive hidden-input inference.
solved_when: Either a construction meeting the above exists — adaptively sound, publicly verifiable SNARGs for an NP-hard family of quantized inference statements from falsifiable standard-model assumptions, with non-black-box reduction and proof/verification complexity polynomial in \(\lambda,\log T\) — or a sharply scoped barrier is established ruling out such constructions.
why: Success would improve the foundational assumptions underlying succinct proofs for hidden-model inference rather than merely optimizing existing proof architectures.
key_works: Craig Gentry, Daniel Wichs (2011), [*Separating Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments From All Falsifiable Assumptions*, ePrint 2010/610](https://eprint.iacr.org/2010/610); Surya Mathialagan et al. (2024), [*Adaptively Sound Zero-Knowledge SNARKs for UP*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/227).

title: Parameter-isolation proofs for prior-task behavior preservation
subfield: Model merging, continual learning, and episodic meta-training
open: Can we certify that adding a new task to a PackNet-style network leaves every prior task's behavior untouched — not just its frozen weights, but also masks, task heads, and mutable inference buffers such as normalization state? Formally, prove identical prior-task outputs under declared arithmetic for 100 tasks sharing a 7B network, with update work proportional to the changed state.
status: PackNet (Mallya & Lazebnik, 2018, arXiv:1711.05769) uses pruning and parameter isolation to protect prior tasks, but frozen weights alone do not cover mutable normalization or other inference state, so no such certification currently exists.
solved_when: A machine-checkable proof establishes that, for 100 tasks sharing a 7B network, prior-task outputs are bit-identical under the declared arithmetic, covering masks, frozen weights, task heads, and every mutable inference buffer used by prior tasks, and that the per-update work is proportional to the changed state.
why: A precise noninterference guarantee supports stronger claims than a sampled forgetting benchmark, which can miss regressions on untested inputs or state not captured by frozen weights alone.
key_works: Arun Mallya, Svetlana Lazebnik (2018), [*PackNet: Adding Multiple Tasks to a Single Network by Iterative Pruning*, arXiv:1711.05769](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.05769).

title: Gaussian-splat visibility and alpha-compositing certificates
subfield: Geometric, implicit, and dynamically parameterized architectures
open: Can a Gaussian-splatting pipeline produce, alongside the rendered image, a compact certificate that its visibility and compositing decisions were correct? Formally, the goal is to prove Gaussian projection, tile membership, depth sorting, opacity, compositing, and every culling/termination decision for a scene of \(10^6\) Gaussians rendered at 1080p.
status: 3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, Drettakis, 2023, arXiv:2308.04079) establishes a sparse learned renderer, but a scene commitment does not certify visibility decisions or delivered pixels.
solved_when: A renderer for \(10^6\) Gaussians at 1080p yields \(O(N+P)\) work for scene size \(N\) and touched splat–tile pairs \(P\), with evidence below 1 MB and certified pixel error.
why: Excluded objects must be accounted for, not merely the splats that were drawn — a scene commitment that certifies only what was composited leaves occluded geometry unverified.
key_works: Bernhard Kerbl, Georgios Kopanas, Thomas Leimkühler, George Drettakis (2023), [*3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering*, arXiv:2308.04079](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04079).

title: On-policy distillation with proved sampling and stop-gradient boundaries
subfield: Distillation and alternative preference objectives
open: Can an on-policy distillation pipeline like GKD be executed end-to-end with verified control flow — proved mixture of fixed and student-generated data, teacher feedback on exactly the sampled sequences, and gradients provably stopped through sampling and the teacher? The goal is a construction demonstrating this for a 7B student distilled from a 70B teacher over \(10^5\) sequences within 10× the runtime of the identical unproved recipe.
status: GKD (Agarwal et al., 2024, arXiv:2306.13649) introduces student-generated distillation and alternative divergences, but does not supply this end-to-end ZK workload.
solved_when: A verified implementation of the GKD recipe (fixed-data/student-generated mixture, teacher feedback on the exact sampled sequences, stop-gradients through sampling and teacher parameters) runs the full workload — 7B student, 70B teacher, \(10^5\) sequences — in under 10× the runtime of the identical unproved recipe.
why: Different sequence sources and differentiation boundaries define genuinely different learning algorithms, so unverified or subtly altered implementations may silently train a different method than intended.
key_works: Rishabh Agarwal et al. (2024), [*On-Policy Distillation of Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes*, arXiv:2306.13649](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13649).

title: Self-paced curriculum inclusion and exclusion certificates
subfield: Data curricula and alternative optimizer state
open: Can a data curriculum prove, round by round, that it admitted and excluded exactly the right examples — including honest evidence about the records it left out? Formally, can each round carry an inclusion and exclusion certificate showing the selected set matches what the committed losses, latent assignments, and pace parameters dictate, even when difficulties and selections are hidden?
status: Self-paced learning (Kumar, Packer, Koller 2010, [Self-Paced Learning for Latent Variable Models](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2010/hash/e57c6b956a6521b28495f2886ca0977a-Abstract.html)) establishes loss-dependent admission of examples, but certification at the proposed private scale additionally requires proving the complete selection, excluded candidates included, which remains unaddressed.
solved_when: A curriculum of \(10^8\) records over 100 rounds is certified, with each round proving both inclusion and exclusion of every candidate according to the committed self-paced rule, while incurring only linear auxiliary work per round and keeping difficulties and selections private.
why: A certificate covering only the selected examples lets the trainer silently drop difficult or inconvenient records; exclusion evidence is what makes the curriculum's selectivity auditable rather than merely asserted.
key_works: M. P. Kumar, Benjamin Packer, Daphne Koller (2010), [*Self-Paced Learning for Latent Variable Models*](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2010/hash/e57c6b956a6521b28495f2886ca0977a-Abstract.html).

title: Private random-reshuffling epoch certificates
subfield: Data curricula and alternative optimizer state
open: Can a data curator prove that each training epoch's record order is a freshly, honestly generated random permutation of all committed record IDs — preserving multiplicities and binding the update order — without revealing the dataset? The target scale is \(10^9\) records across 30 epochs, with linear auxiliary work, under 64 GB of working memory, and explicit assumptions for seed generation and aborts.
status: RandomShuffle theory distinguishes without-replacement epochs from IID sampling [Jeff Haochen, Suvrit Sra (2019), *Random Shuffling Beats SGD after Finite Epochs*](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/haochen19a.html); a permutation-membership proof alone does not establish randomness.
solved_when: A protocol exists that proves per-epoch without-replacement random permutations of all committed IDs (multiplicity-preserving, order-binding) at \(10^9\) records over 30 epochs, using linear auxiliary work and less than 64 GB working memory, with stated seed-generation and abort assumptions.
why: Even when every record appears exactly once per epoch, manipulating the order can change training outcomes — so permuting honestly is itself a property worth certifying.
key_works: Jeff Haochen, Suvrit Sra (2019), [*Random Shuffling Beats SGD after Finite Epochs*](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/haochen19a.html).

title: Muon finite-iteration orthogonalization and shape-scaling proofs
subfield: Data curricula and alternative optimizer state
open: Can the Muon optimizer's exact deployed update — the prescribed finite Newton–Schulz iterations together with its momentum, normalization, shape scaling, and decay — be formally proven correct as specified? The proof must cover the approximation itself, since replacing it with an exact polar factor would certify a different operation.
status: The 2025 scaling work (Jingyuan Liu et al. (2025), [Muon is Scalable for LLM Training, arXiv:2502.16982](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.16982v1)) specifies approximate finite iterations and shape-sensitive scaling; substituting an exact polar factor would certify a different operation.
solved_when: A formal proof certifies Muon's finite-iteration update for \(4{,}096\times16{,}384\) blocks with five Newton–Schulz iterations, running within 10× the optimizer's runtime and using at most two full auxiliary matrix buffers.
why: The finite approximation is part of the optimizer's deployed semantics, so any verification that idealizes it away does not certify what actually runs in training.
key_works: Jingyuan Liu et al. (2025), [*Muon is Scalable for LLM Training*, arXiv:2502.16982](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.16982v1).

title: Adafactor proving without dense second-moment expansion
subfield: Data curricula and alternative optimizer state
open: Can we produce a ZK proof of correct Adafactor optimizer execution whose persistent witness state stays factored, rather than expanding the second moment into a dense matrix? Formally, prove the momentum-free Adafactor variant's row/column accumulators, reconstructed scales, decay, clipping, and relative step size without materializing the dense second-moment tensor.
status: Adafactor reduces optimizer memory through factored second moments (Shazeer & Stern, 2018, arXiv:1804.04235). Preserving that factored saving through the proof system remains additional open work.
solved_when: For 8,192² blocks, the proof system retains O(m+n) persistent optimizer witness state and the auxiliary proof cost is at most 2× the cost of proving the gradient tensor.
why: Adafactor's whole point is sublinear optimizer memory; a dense proof witness negates that principal advantage by reintroducing the memory cost the optimizer was designed to avoid.
key_works: Noam Shazeer, Mitchell Stern (2018), [*Adafactor: Adaptive Learning Rates with Sublinear Memory Cost*, arXiv:1804.04235](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.04235).

title: MeZO paired perturbations and in-place restoration proofs
subfield: Data curricula and alternative optimizer state
open: Can one prove that a MeZO-style memoryless zeroth-order fine-tuning run — seeded directions, paired perturbations, finite-difference loss estimates, in-place restoration, and updates — is correct without ever storing reverse-mode activations? The formal target is a 30B model on a single 80 GB accelerator at below 10× runtime overhead, with the proof certifying loss cancellation and restoration roundoff or exact restoration of committed originals.
status: MeZO demonstrates forward-only fine-tuning, including a 30B single-80-GB-GPU workload without ZK; the corresponding proof-memory and numerical guarantees remain proposed. Key work: Sadhika Malladi et al. (2023), [*Fine-Tuning Language Models with Just Forward Passes*, arXiv:2305.17333](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17333).
solved_when: A machine-checkable proof exists for the full perturb-and-restore sequence on a 30B model running on one 80 GB accelerator at under 10× runtime, certifying either bounded restoration roundoff or exact restoration of the committed original weights, with no reverse-mode activation storage.
why: Floating-point perturb-and-restore sequences need not return exactly to their starting weights, so unproven zeroth-order fine-tuning can silently corrupt model state.
key_works: Sadhika Malladi et al. (2023), [*Fine-Tuning Language Models with Just Forward Passes*, arXiv:2305.17333](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17333).

title: High-dimensional discretized-Gaussian noise certificates
subfield: Diffusion, flow, and iterative-generation proofs
open: Can a verifier certify, from uniform input bits, that a claimed high-dimensional noise vector truly follows a discretized Gaussian with \(2^{20}\) coordinates? Formally: certify sampling on the grid \(2^{-16}\) with support \([-12,12]\) and unit standard deviation per coordinate, with joint total-variation error at most \(2^{-40}\) against the finite law, while binding the sampler's counters and keeping expansion cost at most 2× that of the corresponding uniform-word expansion, with practical PRGs handled by a separate computational argument.
status: Diffusion algorithms specify high-dimensional noise (e.g., DDIM, Jiaming Song et al. 2020, [arXiv:2010.02502](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02502); Tero Karras et al. 2022, [arXiv:2206.00364](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.00364)), but the complete finite-law sampler guarantee remains a proposed extension; moreover, a finite sampler must not be compared with a continuous law in TV distance.
solved_when: A certification protocol exists that, under uniform input bits, certifies \(2^{20}\) noise coordinates with unit standard deviation on grid \(2^{-16}\) over support \([-12,12]\) with joint TV error at most \(2^{-40}\) against the finite law, binds counters and target, and incurs at most 2× the corresponding uniform-word expansion cost, with practical PRGs addressed via a separate computational argument.
why: Correct tensor arithmetic alone cannot protect the output distribution against chosen or correlated latent noise, so without such certificates a diffusion model's noise inputs can be silently manipulated.
key_works: Jiaming Song et al. (2020), [*DDIM*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02502); Tero Karras et al. (2022), [*Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Generative Models*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.00364).

title: Classifier-free guidance branch completeness
subfield: Diffusion, flow, and iterative-generation proofs
open: Prove that in classifier-free guidance, the conditional and unconditional predictions are computed from the same latent and timestep, and that the declared guidance weights and clipping are what actually combine the two branches. Formally, this is a full-trajectory consistency proof for both branches of the guided sampler.
status: Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance (Ho and Salimans, 2022, arXiv:2207.12598) defines the score-combination method; ZK-WAGON (Anantha Ramakrishnan et al., 2025, arXiv:2510.01967) gives selected-layer generation proofs, but does not establish branch consistency over the full trajectory.
solved_when: For a 50-step generation, there is a proof system establishing branch consistency with both branches private, at less than 5% linkage overhead beyond the two denoiser proofs.
why: Altered conditioning or guidance can change the output without changing the advertised checkpoint, so nothing currently pins a guided sampler to its declared guidance recipe.
key_works: Jonathan Ho, Tim Salimans (2022), [*Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance*, arXiv:2207.12598](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.12598); Aadarsh Anantha Ramakrishnan et al. (2025), [*ZK-WAGON*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01967).

title: Denoiser parameterization and sampler-schedule conformance
subfield: Diffusion, flow, and iterative-generation proofs
open: When a diffusion model's denoiser checkpoint is paired with a particular sampler schedule, can we prove — not assume — that the executed computation faithfully matches the declared prediction parameterization, schedule coefficients, timestep selection, preconditioning, and sampler boundaries? The goal is a verified proving layer that certifies this conformance, with exact declared fixed-point semantics.
status: DDIM and EDM define ordinary sampling choices. ZK-WAGON proves selected generation-model layers but leaves complete iterative schedules outside its demonstrated scope.
solved_when: For a 50-step \(1{,}024^2\) latent-diffusion run, the scheduler's proof cost is below 10% of the denoiser's proving time, and the proof certifies prediction-parameterization conversion, schedule coefficients, timestep selection, preconditioning, and sampler boundaries with exact declared fixed-point semantics.
why: The same denoiser checkpoint can implement different generators under different schedules, so without proving the schedule itself one cannot know which generator was actually executed.
key_works: Jiaming Song, Chenlin Meng, Stefano Ermon (2020), [*Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models*, arXiv:2010.02502](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02502); Tero Karras et al. (2022), [*Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Generative Models*, arXiv:2206.00364](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.00364); Aadarsh Anantha Ramakrishnan et al. (2025), [*ZK-WAGON*, arXiv:2510.01967](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01967).

title: Adaptive high-order diffusion-solver transition proofs
subfield: Diffusion, flow, and iterative-generation proofs
open: How can a proof system certify that an adaptive high-order diffusion ODE solver, such as DPM-Solver, actually executed its adaptive logic correctly — including rejected steps, local error estimates, step-size updates, reused derivatives, and the final-time boundary?
status: DPM-Solver supplies high-order diffusion ODE methods, but proving its adaptive execution must account for rejected work and a declared numerical tolerance; no such proof system currently exists.
solved_when: A verifiable proof covers accepted and rejected adaptive steps, local error estimates, step-size updates, reused derivatives, and final-time boundaries across 10–200 denoiser evaluations, with proof work proportional to the actual number of evaluations and less than 20% control/error-check overhead, and with a declared numerical tolerance.
why: Valid denoiser calls alone do not establish that the integrator used them correctly; without certifying the adaptive logic, a purported sampling trace could hide incorrect step acceptance or error control.
key_works: Cheng Lu et al. (2022), [*DPM-Solver: A Fast ODE Solver for Diffusion Probabilistic Model Sampling in Around 10 Steps*, arXiv:2206.00927](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.00927).

title: Latent-to-pixel VAE decoding with complete output binding
subfield: Diffusion, flow, and iterative-generation proofs
open: Can a verifiable pipeline cover the entire path from a diffusion model's final latent to the pixels a user actually sees — the latent rescaling, the full learned VAE decoding, upsampling, clipping, and byte quantization — so that a proof of the latent implies correctness of the delivered image?
status: Latent Diffusion (Robin Rombach et al., 2022; preprint 2021, arXiv:2112.10752) separates denoising from image decoding via a learned VAE decoder, and a proof of the final latent does not establish correctness of the displayed image bytes.
solved_when: A proof system verifies the complete latent-to-pixel pipeline at 1,024² resolution, with proof evidence below 1 MB and at least 4× reduction in peak witness memory compared to retaining all decoder activations.
why: Without proof through the final representation conversion, output substitution remains possible: a proof of the final latent does not establish correctness of the displayed image bytes.
key_works: Robin Rombach et al. (2022; preprint 2021), [*High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models*, arXiv:2112.10752](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10752).

title: ControlNet conditioning and residual-injection certificates
subfield: Diffusion, flow, and iterative-generation proofs
open: Can a verifier certify, for a ControlNet-guided generation, that the control image, its preprocessing, each conditioning tower, and every scaled residual injection followed the declared timestep schedule? Formally, the goal is a proof system binding these conditioning interfaces to the committed schedule parameters.
status: ControlNet (Zhang, Rao, Agrawala, 2023, arXiv:2302.05543) supplies the spatial-conditioning architecture, but proving separate networks does not automatically certify their conditioning interfaces.
solved_when: For three controls and 50 steps, the certificate incurs less than 10% interface overhead while exactly enforcing start, stop, and strength settings.
why: Omitting or altering a control changes the contracted generator even with authentic base weights, so conditioning interfaces are the gap between verified weights and verified outputs.
key_works: Lvmin Zhang, Anyi Rao, Maneesh Agrawala (2023), [*Adding Conditional Control to Text-to-Image Diffusion Models*, arXiv:2302.05543](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05543).

title: Masked-diffusion token update and stopping proofs
subfield: Diffusion, flow, and iterative-generation proofs
open: Can we produce machine-checkable evidence that a masked-diffusion language model's generation followed its declared rules — bidirectional updates, confidence-based token selection, re-masking quotas, immutable prompt regions, and stopping at a declared length? Formally, the goal is a proof system whose evidence stays under 1 MB for 1,024 output positions and up to 128 rounds, with verification work proportional only to the positions declared as evaluated.
status: LLaDA establishes masked-diffusion language modeling, and iLLaMA (Nie et al., 2025, arXiv:2502.09992) extends it with further generation capabilities. Existing autoregressive proof statements do not automatically cover the revisable, multi-position intermediate states that masked diffusion produces.
solved_when: A verifier accepts certified traces of bidirectional round updates, confidence selection, re-masking quotas, prompt immutability, and variable-length stopping for 1,024 output positions and up to 128 rounds, with evidence below 1 MB and computational cost scaling with the number of declared evaluated positions.
why: Hidden re-masking, premature stopping, or silent edits to the prompt region can change a model's output even when every forward pass is honestly computed, so forward-pass validity alone does not guarantee the reported generation.
key_works: Shen Nie et al. (2025), [*Large Language Diffusion Models*, arXiv:2502.09992](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09992); Shen Nie et al. (2026), [*Improved Large Language Diffusion Models*, arXiv:2606.25331](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25331).

title: AOT distributional preference matching with private ranks
subfield: Distillation and alternative preference objectives
open: Can a federated group of workers, each holding private preference rankings, prove that the empirical reward distributions fed into an AOT alignment step are exactly the ones their local data warrants — sorted independently, matched by optimal transport, with tie subgradients handled correctly — without ever revealing the ranks themselves?
status: AOT derives distributional alignment through one-dimensional optimal transport (Igor Melnyk et al. (2024), [*Distributional Preference Alignment of LLMs via Optimal Transport*, arXiv:2406.05882](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.05882)), but an empirical proof does not establish population stochastic dominance — no protocol currently combines the matching pipeline with private ranks.
solved_when: A verifiable protocol completes an AOT update over 8,192 examples distributed across 128 workers, with \(O(B\log B)\) auxiliary work per batch, hiding all individual ranks while proving complete empirical reward distributions, independent sorts, optimal-transport matching, and tie subgradients.
why: If workers can drop observations or silently alter ranks, the distributional objective being optimized is not the one intended, and the alignment guarantee of AOT is void; privacy plus verifiability is what makes the method safe to federate.
key_works: Igor Melnyk et al. (2024), [*Distributional Preference Alignment of LLMs via Optimal Transport*, arXiv:2406.05882](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.05882).

title: Full-vocabulary temperature-distillation gradient proofs
subfield: Distillation and alternative preference objectives
open: Can a student model prove that its update was distilled from a committed teacher's full distribution, without revealing that distribution? Formally, produce a verifiable proof that the update used the teacher's full temperature-scaled softmax distribution, the temperature-squared loss factor, the hard-label mixture, and the resulting student update, over a 128K-entry vocabulary and 2K-token sequences, within 3× the cost of the constituent forward/backward proofs.
status: Classical distillation (Geoffrey Hinton, Oriol Vinyals, Jeff Dean (2015), [*Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network*, arXiv:1503.02531](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531)) supplies the objective, and zkDL (Haochen Sun et al. (2023), [*zkDL*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.16273)) supplies training-proof primitives; their complete hidden-teacher integration at this scale remains a proposed target.
solved_when: A proof system exists that proves use of the committed teacher's full temperature-scaled distribution, temperature-squared loss factor, hard-label mixture, and student update, handling 128K-vocabulary, 2K-token sequences at total cost at most 3× that of the required constituent forward/backward proofs, while hiding teacher probabilities.
why: A top-k approximation of the teacher distribution can differ materially from the full distribution named in a training contract, so verifiers currently cannot confirm that contract terms were honored exactly.
key_works: Geoffrey Hinton, Oriol Vinyals, Jeff Dean (2015), [*Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network*, arXiv:1503.02531](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531); Haochen Sun et al. (2023), [*zkDL*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.16273).

title: Algebraic cryptanalysis of fully bound numerical transcripts
subfield: Fiat–Shamir and concrete-hash foundations
open: How does the security of Poseidon/Poseidon2-based Fiat–Shamir challenge generation actually hold up when the hash is exercised against real sumcheck and low-degree verification equations rather than in isolation — can a reproducible experimental attack frontier be built that exposes genuine weaknesses in fully bound numerical transcripts? The target is a systematic, reproducible study coupling the algebraic hash to live verifier equations, distinguishing mere challenge bias from outright acceptance of a false statement.
status: The 2026 Poseidon-based Fiat–Shamir study (Hovhannisyan, Asaturyan, Hovhannisyan, *Cryptanalysis of Poseidon-Based Fiat-Shamir Protocols*, ePrint 2026/409) reports no meaningful forgeries, even with heavily reduced parameters; its negative experiments leave substantial room for broader, independently replicated analysis.
solved_when: A reproducible attack framework exists that couples Poseidon/Poseidon2 challenge generation with actual sumcheck and low-degree verification equations and covers at least 100 field/width/round configurations, including deployed full-round configurations, with results that discriminate challenge bias from acceptance of a false statement.
why: Algebraic hashes and algebraic verifier equations may interact differently than isolated hash benchmarks suggest, so concrete security claims for Fiat–Shamir instantiations over Poseidon remain untested until the coupling is studied directly.
key_works: Hayk Hovhannisyan, Nerses Asaturyan, Gohar Hovhannisyan (2026), [*Cryptanalysis of Poseidon-Based Fiat-Shamir Protocols*, ePrint 2026/409](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/409).

title: Quantum security loss for unmodified tensor sumcheck transcripts
subfield: Fiat–Shamir and concrete-hash foundations
open: How much quantum security is lost when the standard Fiat–Shamir transform is applied, unchanged, to an \(m\)-round, degree-\(d\) tensor sumcheck protocol? Specifically, prove a QROM security loss of \(O(q^2\operatorname{poly}(m,d))\), or exhibit a protocol-specific obstruction showing such a bound is impossible.
status: General multi-round reductions can incur substantial round-dependent losses. Improved modified transforms exist, leaving the precise frontier for the unchanged tensor protocol as the target.
solved_when: Either a proof establishes QROM security loss \(O(q^2\operatorname{poly}(m,d))\) for ordinary Fiat–Shamir on the unmodified tensor sumcheck, or a protocol-specific obstruction is established — in either case covering \(m\le64\), \(d\le8\), and quantum hash-query budget \(q\), without substituting a different transform.
why: A quantum-resistant commitment primitive alone does not confer a complete quantum soundness bound; without this result, concrete quantum security claims for unmodified tensor sumcheck-based SNARKs rest on an unquantified gap.
key_works: Jelle Don, Serge Fehr, Christian Majenz (2020), [*The Measure-and-Reprogram Technique 2.0: Multi-Round Fiat-Shamir and More*, arXiv:2003.05207](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.05207); Thomas Attema et al. (2026), [*The Fiat–Shamir Transformation of \((\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_\mu)\)-Special-Sound Interactive Proofs*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-025-09569-y).

title: Practical straight-line extraction transforms for numerical PIOPs
subfield: Fiat–Shamir and concrete-hash foundations
open: Can straight-line-extractable transforms be made practical for 32–64-round tensor PIOPs, with all transcript and recomputation costs accounted for? The target is to specialize these transforms so that they incur at most 2× prover work and 1.25× proof bytes relative to ordinary Fiat–Shamir, together with an explicit bound on polynomial extraction time.
status: Rotem and Tessaro (2025; preprint 2024, [*Straight-Line Knowledge Extraction for Multi-Round Protocols*, ePrint 2024/1724](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1724)) already give multi-round transforms, including a QROM-secure variant; the open target concerns concrete numerical-proof overhead rather than existence of such transforms.
solved_when: A construction specialized to 32–64-round tensor PIOPs is given whose full accounting — including transcript and recomputation costs — stays within 2× prover work and 1.25× proof bytes relative to ordinary Fiat–Shamir, and whose polynomial extraction time is explicitly stated.
why: Efficient extraction would simplify recursive security arguments without making proving prohibitively expensive.
key_works: Lior Rotem, Stefano Tessaro (2025; preprint 2024), [*Straight-Line Knowledge Extraction for Multi-Round Protocols*, ePrint 2024/1724](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1724).

title: Point-cloud sampling and set-abstraction certificates
subfield: Geometric, implicit, and dynamically parameterized architectures
open: Can the core geometric sampling and set-abstraction pipeline of PointNet++-style models — farthest-point sampling, radius/neighbor grouping, duplicate handling, relative coordinates, and full feature aggregation — be proven correct end-to-end? The target is to prove a pipeline with 10^5 points, 1,024 centers, and three abstraction levels in under one minute, with subquadratic work and exactly the declared selection rules.
status: PointNet++ supplies hierarchical set abstraction (Charles R. Qi, Li Yi, Hao Su, Leonidas J. Guibas, 2017, arXiv:1706.02413), but generic tensor proofs do not automatically establish geometric neighborhood selection.
solved_when: A proof system certifies farthest-point sampling, radius/neighbor grouping, duplicates, relative coordinates, and complete feature aggregation for 10^5 input points, 1,024 centers, and three abstraction levels, with total proving time below one minute, subquadratic work, and selection rules matching exactly those declared.
why: Even when features are computed correctly on the chosen neighborhoods, the wrong neighborhoods can be selected — so a verified model can still misrepresent the advertised one; certificates for the sampling layer close this gap.
key_works: Charles R. Qi, Li Yi, Hao Su, Leonidas J. Guibas (2017), [*PointNet++: Deep Hierarchical Feature Learning on Point Sets in a Metric Space*, arXiv:1706.02413](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02413).

title: Efficient uniqueness certificates for trained deep-equilibrium models
subfield: Geometric, implicit, and dynamically parameterized architectures
open: Can we cheaply certify, on real trained deep-equilibrium networks, that the fixed point the solver reached is the intended one? Formally, on a pinned corpus of 100 trained \(10^5\)-dimensional implicit networks, produce invariant domains and uniqueness/stability certificates covering at least 80% of them, using 10× less proving work than replaying the solver.
status: Deep Equilibrium Models (Shaojie Bai, J. Zico Kolter, Vladlen Koltun, 2019, arXiv:1909.01377) established implicit inference, and the contraction residual bound is standard. Efficient certification on actual trained networks, with useful coverage, is the proposed gap.
solved_when: At least 80 of the 100 pinned networks carry a certified useful invariant domain and uniqueness/stability conditions, the certification costs at most one-tenth of the work of replaying the solver, the residual bound \(\epsilon\le(1-L)10^{-4}\) holds whenever the contraction factor satisfies \(L<1\), and unsupported cases fall back rather than claim a certificate.
why: A cheap residual certificate is valuable only when it identifies the intended solution; without efficient uniqueness checks, verification of implicit inference remains either vacuous or prohibitively expensive.
key_works: Shaojie Bai, J. Zico Kolter, Vladlen Koltun (2019), [*Deep Equilibrium Models*, arXiv:1909.01377](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.01377).

title: NeRF hierarchical ray-sampling and compositing proofs
subfield: Geometric, implicit, and dynamically parameterized architectures
open: Can a NeRF's full rendering pipeline — camera rays, hierarchical coarse-to-fine sample probabilities, radiance and density evaluations, and transmittance compositing — be bound into a single succinct proof? Formally, the goal is a zk/verifiable circuit that certifies the rendered image end-to-end, so that neither the camera, the sampling, nor the compositing can be altered without detection.
status: NeRF (Ben Mildenhall et al. (2020), [*NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis*, arXiv:2003.08934](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.08934)) combines a learned scene function with hierarchical sampling and volume rendering; no existing result certifies the rendered image beyond the network evaluations themselves.
solved_when: For a \(512^2\) image rendered with 64 coarse and 128 fine samples per ray, there is verifiable evidence of size below 1 MB, witness memory reduced 4× relative to the naive approach, and an explicit bound on pixel error between the proven and true renderings.
why: Network evaluations alone do not certify the rendered image; without binding the whole pipeline, camera substitution, sample omission, and altered compositing remain outside isolated neural proofs.
key_works: Ben Mildenhall et al. (2020), [*NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis*, arXiv:2003.08934](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.08934).

title: Hypernetwork-generated weight integrity without repeated full commitments
subfield: Geometric, implicit, and dynamically parameterized architectures
open: Can a verifier be convinced that every transient weight block in a hypernetwork-driven system was produced by the committed hypernetwork and used exactly at the occurrences its computation graph prescribes — including authorized reuse and aliasing — without ever committing to the fully materialized weights? Formally, this asks for a proof of provenance and usage integrity for generated parameters against a static commitment to the generator.
status: HyperNetworks (David Ha, Andrew Dai, Quoc V. Le, 2016, *HyperNetworks*, arXiv:1609.09106) generate one network's weights using another network. Static checkpoint commitments do not cover the transient parameter relations such generation creates; no existing technique proves integrity of these transient weights without repeated materialization.
solved_when: For a workload of 1,000 transient weight blocks totaling \(10^8\) weights, the scheme proves correct generation and graph-prescribed consumption (covering reuse and aliasing) with less than 10% interface overhead and verifier memory below one tenth of the full generated tensor.
why: Input-dependent generated parameters currently have no provenance or usage guarantees, and naive solutions require repeatedly materializing and committing to the full weight tensor, which is prohibitively expensive; a cheap integrity proof makes dynamically parameterized models auditable against their committed generator.
key_works: David Ha, Andrew Dai, Quoc V. Le (2016), [*HyperNetworks*, arXiv:1609.09106](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.09106).

title: Detector proposal suppression and score-update completeness
subfield: Geometric, implicit, and dynamically parameterized architectures
open: Can we produce a single machine-checkable certificate that a detector's full postprocessing stage — proposal decoding, thresholding, IoU comparisons, tie handling, and every NMS or Soft-NMS score update through to the final boxes — was carried out correctly? Formally, the certificate must prove the entire suppression pipeline, not just selected slices of it.
status: Soft-NMS (Bodla et al., 2017, arXiv:1704.04503) defines the iterative suppression procedure whose correctness must be certified. DSperse (Ivanov et al., 2026) evaluates selected detector slices while relying on external mechanisms for global consistency; complete postprocessing verification remains an open, distinct problem.
solved_when: For a workload of 30,000 proposals and 80 classes, the certificate proves all suppression decisions in under one second, with exact agreement on 10,000 adversarial boundary fixtures.
why: Without completeness at the postprocessing stage, valid proofs of the detector layers can coexist with detections that were selectively suppressed or added after the fact, so the attested output no longer reflects what the network actually produced.
key_works: Navaneeth Bodla et al. (2017), [*Soft-NMS—Improving Object Detection With One Line of Code*, arXiv:1704.04503](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.04503); Dan Ivanov et al. (2026), [*Targeted Zero-Knowledge Verification for Computer Vision Inference*](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-032-29558-3_14).

title: Canonical proof-encoding contracts
subfield: Implementation security of numerical proof services
open: Can we give numerical proof services a single canonical contract — injective encodings and protocol-specific validity rules for fields, points, tensor shapes, and proof lengths — that holds uniformly across five independent implementations?
status: Wright's 2022 disclosures documented invalid-value acceptance in specialized proofs, and those fixed defects provide context; uniform machine-checked proof-decoding contracts remain the proposed target, with the Rust-to-Lean verification pipeline of Klaus et al. (2026) as a relevant tool.
solved_when: A parser-to-algebra refinement is proved, and 10 million adversarial encodings are released with no unresolved representation-dependent acceptance across the five implementations.
why: Malformed bytes can defeat assumptions that are implicit in an algebraic verifier description, so acceptance decisions silently diverge from the intended math.
key_works: Opal Wright (2022), [*Specialized Zero-Knowledge Proof failures*](https://blog.trailofbits.com/2022/11/29/specialized-zero-knowledge-proof-failures/); Natalia Klaus et al. (2026), [*A Rust-to-Lean Verification Pipeline with AI Provers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30106).

title: Typed Fiat–Shamir transcript generation
subfield: Implementation security of numerical proof services
open: Can we generate Fiat–Shamir transcript codecs and challenge schedules automatically from — and checked against — a separately reviewed dependency specification that binds checkpoints, inputs, numerical modes, and sessions? The goal is a verified generator rather than hand-audited bindings across composed protocols.
status: Merlin provides transcript framing and domain separation, and the Frozen Heart disclosures (Jim Miller, 2022) demonstrated the consequences of omitted bindings in Girault, Bulletproofs, and PlonK. The remaining target is verified dependency generation, not rediscovery of patched defects.
solved_when: A generated implementation covers 50 composed subprotocols and survives one million substitution mutations with no unexplained acceptance, with all bindings verified against the dependency specification.
why: Application-specific statement bindings must remain complete as protocols and APIs evolve; a verified generator removes the class of omitted-binding vulnerabilities that hand-maintained transcripts invite.
key_works: Merlin contributors, [*Merlin Transcripts*](https://merlin.cool/), documentation accessed 2026; Jim Miller (2022), [*Coordinated disclosure of vulnerabilities affecting Girault, Bulletproofs, and PlonK*](https://blog.trailofbits.com/2022/04/13/part-1-coordinated-disclosure-of-vulnerabilities-affecting-girault-bulletproofs-and-plonk/).

title: Executable verifier refinement
subfield: Implementation security of numerical proof services
open: Can we mechanically prove that each of three deployed numerical-proof verifiers accepts exactly the computations its mathematical specification prescribes, so that the running code and the spec are formally the same object? The effort should span decoding, transcript handling, field arithmetic, and commitment checks, and the machine-checked acceptance equivalence should run within reasonable engineering budgets.
status: The 2026 Rust-to-Lean experience report of Klaus, Conejero, and Tolmach (arXiv:2605.30106) verifies selected Plonky3 and RISC Zero primitives; whole-verifier refinement across three systems remains a larger, unattempted target.
solved_when: Machine-checked acceptance equivalence is established for all three deployed numerical-proof verifiers, covering decoding, transcripts, field arithmetic, and commitment checks, with at most 20% runtime overhead and an explicit enumeration of extraction, compiler, and hardware assumptions.
why: Correct circuit mathematics is insufficient when the accepting software implements a different verifier: a mismatch between spec and executable silently undermines every soundness guarantee the proof system is assumed to provide.
key_works: Natalia Klaus, Juan Conejero, Palina Tolmach (2026), [*A Rust-to-Lean Verification Pipeline with AI Provers: An Experience Report*, arXiv:2605.30106](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30106).

title: Measured soft-error resilience of GPU proving
subfield: Implementation security of numerical proof services
open: How resilient are GPU-based proof systems to single-bit hardware faults encountered in practice? Run a measured fault-injection campaign — one million documented single-bit faults across witness generation, algebraic proving, and commitments on three GPU stacks — and quantify false-claim acceptance against fixed authenticated public inputs under a fault-free verifier.
status: SASSIFI (Siva Hari et al., 2017, [*SASSIFI: An Architecture-level Fault Injection Tool for GPU Application Resilience Evaluation*](https://research.nvidia.com/publication/2017-04_sassifi-architecture-level-fault-injection-tool-gpu-application-resilience)) supplies GPU fault-injection methods, and ZKProphet (Tarunesh Verma et al., 2025, [*ZKProphet*, arXiv:2509.22684](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22684)) characterizes prover performance; however, their combination does not establish this proof-service resilience campaign.
solved_when: The campaign is completed with all quantitative targets met: one million single-bit faults injected and documented, at most 2% fault-free overhead, and retention of at least 90% of valid completed work after localization.
why: Corrupted witnesses, changed public claims, and compromised verifiers carry different implications and recovery costs, so empirical measurements distinguish which failure modes actually matter in deployed proof services.
key_works: Siva Hari et al. (2017), [*SASSIFI: An Architecture-level Fault Injection Tool for GPU Application Resilience Evaluation*](https://research.nvidia.com/publication/2017-04_sassifi-architecture-level-fault-injection-tool-gpu-application-resilience); Tarunesh Verma et al. (2025), [*ZKProphet*, arXiv:2509.22684](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22684).

title: Proof-stack build-to-deployment binding
subfield: Implementation security of numerical proof services
open: Can the full chain from reviewed source through dependencies, compiler flags, generated circuits, and keys to the deployed verifier binary be bound into a single piece of reproducible release evidence? Formally, the goal is a mechanism that ties all of these layers together so any divergence between what was reviewed and what is running can be detected.
status: SLSA specifies build provenance, and Rust-to-Lean supplies selected code-verification examples; however, connecting those assurances across a complete proof release remains additional work.
solved_when: A demonstration covers 100 configurations across three builders, producing either bit-identical artifacts or justified, documented nondeterminism, and rejecting unsupported substitutions.
why: Clients currently have no reliable way to determine whether the deployed checker corresponds to the proof system that was actually reviewed; such binding closes that trust gap.
key_works: SLSA contributors, [*Build: Provenance*, v1.2](https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.2/build-provenance), accessed 2026; Natalia Klaus et al. (2026), [*A Rust-to-Lean Verification Pipeline with AI Provers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30106).

title: Cross-tenant witness lifetime and zeroization
subfield: Implementation security of numerical proof services
open: How can a numerical proof service guarantee that a private witness is truly gone after use, across every place it can linger — CPU memory, GPU scratch and spill buffers, temporary files, in-flight cancellation, and reused workers? Formally, this asks for enforced witness lifetime and zeroization across a whole multi-tenant device/runtime stack.
status: LeftoverLocals (Sorensen and Khlaaf, 2024, arXiv:2401.16603) demonstrated memory recovery on affected Apple, Qualcomm, and AMD GPUs, motivating lifecycle assurance — though this does not imply every GPU remains vulnerable, nor that tests prove physical erasure.
solved_when: On three declared device/runtime combinations, one million tenant transitions are tested with no recovered residuals and less than 1% throughput overhead, supported by a conditional noninterference argument.
why: Transcript-level zero knowledge does not protect a witness left in memory that a later tenant can read; without lifecycle enforcement, the proof system leaks the very secret it proves about.
key_works: Tyler Sorensen, Heidy Khlaaf (2024), [*LeftoverLocals: Listening to LLM Responses Through Leaked GPU Local Memory*, arXiv:2401.16603](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.16603).

title: Fisher-weighted merging with proved information estimators
subfield: Model merging, continual learning, and episodic meta-training
open: Can a Fisher-weighted model-merging pipeline be built so that every step — from sample construction and squared-score accumulation through damping, weighted merging, and the treatment of zero denominators — comes with a machine-checkable proof, with a stated choice of predictive versus empirical Fisher information? The goal is a verified estimator whose justification is carried by the proof itself, not merely plausible merge weights.
status: Fisher-weighted merging currently relies on posterior-precision approximations, following Matena and Raffel (2022), *Merging Models with Fisher-Weighted Averaging* (arXiv:2111.09832), but arbitrary positive merge weights are not evidence of a correctly computed Fisher estimate.
solved_when: The full pipeline is verified over eight 7B models, with auxiliary proof cost below 2× the cost of the underlying score-gradient proofs and merge arithmetic, and with the predictive-versus-empirical Fisher choice explicitly specified.
why: The weighting estimator encodes the justification for the merge; without verified estimation, arbitrary positive merge weights give no evidence that the Fisher estimate was computed correctly.
key_works: Michael Matena, Colin Raffel (2022), [*Merging Models with Fisher-Weighted Averaging*, arXiv:2111.09832](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.09832).

title: TIES trimming, sign election, and survivor-denominator proofs
subfield: Model merging, continual learning, and episodic meta-training
open: Can the full TIES-Merging pipeline — magnitude trimming of task vectors, sign election, and averaging over the surviving coordinates, including the tie-breaking rule when no coordinate survives — be executed verifiably on private model weights? The target is merging 16 private 7B models with a zero-knowledge proof of every stage costing at most 3× that of proving weighted averaging over the same committed weights.
status: TIES-Merging (Prateek Yadav et al., 2023, *TIES-Merging: Resolving Interference When Merging Models*, arXiv:2306.01708) establishes the three-stage merge algorithm itself. The matched private proof for that pipeline and the comparative cost target remain open.
solved_when: A proof system exists that verifies magnitude trimming, sign election, survivor selection, averaging over the correct survivors, and the zero-survivor rule for merging 16 private 7B models, at total proof cost within 3× the cost of proving weighted averaging over the same committed weights.
why: Without an end-to-end proof, a provider can manipulate contributor inputs or the survivor denominators while still reporting a plausible merged checkpoint, so the merged model's provenance cannot be trusted.
key_works: Prateek Yadav et al. (2023), [*TIES-Merging: Resolving Interference When Merging Models*, arXiv:2306.01708](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01708).

title: Synaptic-intelligence path-integral consolidation proofs
subfield: Model merging, continual learning, and episodic meta-training
open: Can we produce, for the full Synaptic Intelligence procedure, a verifiable proof that every prescribed quantity — the gradient–parameter-change products accumulated along the optimization path, the task-boundary normalization, damping, and reset steps, and the consolidation penalties applied afterward — was computed as specified? In other words, certify the path-dependent computation itself, not just the final weights.
status: Synaptic Intelligence (Zenke, Poole, Ganguli, 2017, *Continual Learning Through Synaptic Intelligence*, arXiv:1703.04200) accumulates importance estimates along the optimization path; no current result proves that this accumulator certifiably yields the prescribed values, let alone guarantees absence of forgetting.
solved_when: A proof system covers all SI consolidation steps and scales to 1B parameters across 100 tasks, with less than 5% extra proof cost and persistent verifier state that grows only linearly with the parameter count.
why: Final weights alone cannot establish how path-dependent importance values were obtained, so without such proofs an auditor cannot distinguish genuine SI consolidation from arbitrary importance values attached to the same weights.
key_works: Friedemann Zenke, Ben Poole, Surya Ganguli (2017), [*Continual Learning Through Synaptic Intelligence*, arXiv:1703.04200](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.04200).

title: GEM projection feasibility and optimality certificates
subfield: Model merging, continual learning, and episodic meta-training
open: Can Gradient Episodic Memory's projection step be fully certified — that is, can one prove that the quadratic program over all required prior-task gradients was solved correctly, with feasibility, stationarity, complementary slackness, and a certified objective gap of at most \(10^{-6}(1+\|g\|^2)\) — at practical scale, targeting 100 prior tasks and 100M parameters at below 2× auxiliary cost over gradient proofs?
status: GEM (Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017, arXiv:1706.08840) supplies the constrained-update algorithm, but its first-order constraints do not guarantee exact non-increase of every nonlinear task loss, and no certified optimality proof for the projection QP exists.
solved_when: A verifiable proof system establishes feasibility, stationarity, and complementary slackness for GEM's gradient-projection QP using all required prior-task gradients, with certified objective gap at most \(10^{-6}(1+\|g\|^2)\), demonstrated at 100 prior tasks and 100M parameters with auxiliary proving cost below 2× that of gradient proofs.
why: Feasibility alone cannot certify that the intended projection was computed; without optimality certificates, a verifier cannot distinguish a genuine GEM update from an arbitrary feasible one.
key_works: David Lopez-Paz, Marc’Aurelio Ranzato (2017), [*Gradient Episodic Memory for Continual Learning*, arXiv:1706.08840](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.08840).

title: Meta-training episode isolation and support/query dataflow
subfield: Model merging, continual learning, and episodic meta-training
open: Can a meta-training run certify, at the level of individual episodes, that no information flows between them — that each episode in a MAML meta-batch genuinely starts from the prescribed initialization with fresh optimizer and normalization state, and that inner-loop updates never see query data?
status: MAML (Finn, Abbeel, Levine 2017, [arXiv:1703.03400](https://arXiv.org/abs/1703.03400)) establishes task-specific adaptation, but complete episode-state isolation has not been addressed; it is distinct from merely proving higher derivatives, and no existing work certifies it.
solved_when: A proof system verifies, across \(10^6\) episodes, that every episode starts from the prescribed initialization and episode-local optimizer/normalization state, certifies support/query disjointness and the absence of query influence on inner updates, all with less than 5% overhead beyond the cost of gradient proofs.
why: Hidden state carried between episodes can leak adaptation information and silently alter evaluation semantics, so without such proofs the meaning of meta-learned adaptation results is not trustworthy.
key_works: Chelsea Finn, Pieter Abbeel, Sergey Levine (2017), [*Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning for Fast Adaptation of Deep Networks*, arXiv:1703.03400](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.03400).

title: Interleaved-image cross-attention routing proofs
subfield: Multimodal input, alignment, and output proofs
open: Can we prove that each text token in an interleaved image–text model attends only to its permitted media states — including sentinels, gated cross-attention, and encoder-state reuse — so that cross-modal source selection is verifiably correct? Formally, for 64 media items and 8,192 text positions, produce exact attention masks with less than 5% routing overhead beyond the attention arithmetic.
status: Flamingo (Jean-Baptiste Alayrac et al. (2022), [*Flamingo: a Visual Language Model for Few-Shot Learning*, arXiv:2204.14198](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.14198)) makes interleaved visual/text sequences explicit, but generic attention proofs do not automatically bind cross-modal source selection.
solved_when: A proof system verifies the permitted image/video state assignments for every text token at the stated scale — 64 media items and 8,192 text positions — with exact masks and routing overhead below 5% beyond attention arithmetic.
why: Without such proofs, a provider could attach valid features from the wrong image to a text position, making the output appear well-formed while derived from unauthorized cross-modal sources.
key_works: Jean-Baptiste Alayrac et al. (2022), [*Flamingo: a Visual Language Model for Few-Shot Learning*, arXiv:2204.14198](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.14198).

title: Dynamic-resolution image patch and merger conformance
subfield: Multimodal input, alignment, and output proofs
open: Can we prove that a vision–language model's dynamic-resolution image pipeline is faithful — that every decoded image is resized, cut into patches, assigned to attention windows, spatially merged, and fed to the language model in exactly the way the model specification prescribes? Formally, this asks for a zk proof system certifying pixel resizing, patch coordinates, window assignment, spatial merging, and vision-to-language token ordering under dynamic resolutions.
status: Qwen2.5-VL specifies dynamic-resolution processing, and ZKTorch provides composable ML proof blocks; complete spatial-coverage certification is the remaining extension.
solved_when: A proof system certifies the full preprocessing and merging pipeline — resizing, patch coordinates, window assignment, spatial merging, and token ordering — with exact coordinate rules, covering 1,000 adversarial image dimensions up to \(4{,}096^2\), while keeping preprocessing/merging proving time below 20% of vision-tower proving time.
why: An authentic vision tower can still receive the wrong crop, patch ordering, or image coverage, so model correctness proofs are meaningless without certifying the image pipeline that feeds it.
key_works: Shuai Bai et al. (2025), [*Qwen2.5-VL Technical Report*, arXiv:2502.13923](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13923); Bing-Jyue Chen, Lilia Tang, Daniel Kang (2025), [*ZKTorch*, arXiv:2507.07031](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07031).

title: Learned visual resampler proofs with complete patch coverage
subfield: Multimodal input, alignment, and output proofs
open: Certify Q-Former or Perceiver-style resampling, binding learned queries, attention masks, projections, and ordering to committed visual features. Compress 4,096 visual tokens to 32–64 query tokens with at least 4× less peak witness memory than materializing all attention tensors.
status: BLIP-2 and Flamingo establish learned visual-compression architectures. They do not provide these ZK implementations.
why: Compression can hide omitted visual regions unless its complete input relation is proved.
key_works: Junnan Li et al. (2023), [*BLIP-2*, arXiv:2301.12597](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12597); Jean-Baptiste Alayrac et al. (2022), [*Flamingo*, arXiv:2204.14198](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.14198).

title: Waveform-to-log-Mel front-end certificates
subfield: Multimodal input, alignment, and output proofs
open: Can the entire waveform-to-log-Mel front-end — channel mixing, resampling, padding, STFT, Mel filtering, log clipping, and normalization — be proven correct against committed PCM audio? Formally, the question is whether a verifiable certificate binds the log-Mel features fed to a speech encoder to the committed original recording.
status: Whisper's paper and implementation define the ordinary signal-processing path, and any complete proof must include the preprocessing often left outside the neural circuit — see Alec Radford et al. (2022), [*Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision*, arXiv:2212.04356](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04356), and OpenAI Whisper contributors, [*audio.py*](https://github.com/openai/whisper/blob/main/whisper/audio.py).
solved_when: A proof system covers channel mixing, resampling, padding, STFT, Mel filtering, log clipping, and normalization from committed PCM, meeting the quantitative targets: under 10 seconds proving for 60 seconds of 48-kHz stereo audio, a published spectrogram-error bound, and 10,000 framing-edge fixtures.
why: Proving the encoder alone does not bind its input features to the original recording; without a certified front-end, the connection between the log-Mel spectrogram and the actual audio remains unverified.
key_works: Alec Radford et al. (2022), [*Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision*, arXiv:2212.04356](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04356); OpenAI Whisper contributors, [*audio.py*](https://github.com/openai/whisper/blob/main/whisper/audio.py).

title: Variable-frame-rate audio-video time correspondence
subfield: Multimodal input, alignment, and output proofs
open: When a multimodal system consumes a variable-frame-rate video stream together with its audio, can it prove that every frame, audio chunk, and modality interleaving it used is anchored to the correct point on a single timeline — even when frames are dropped or repeated, and timestamps must be converted to positions? Formally, the problem is to construct a verifiable certificate covering frame selection, audio chunking, modality interleaving, and timestamp-to-position conversion.
status: Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen2.5-Omni (Shuai Bai et al. (2025), *Qwen2.5-VL Technical Report*; Jin Xu et al. (2025), *Qwen2.5-Omni Technical Report*) specify temporal and multimodal mechanisms, but proving chronology and routing remains an additional obligation.
solved_when: A certificate exists that, on one-hour variable-frame-rate streams, guarantees no undeclared timestamp reassignment and incurs less than 10% alignment-proof overhead, while accounting for dropped and repeated frames.
why: Correct per-modality inference can still combine observations from incompatible times, so without such a certificate an apparently sound multimodal answer may rest on temporally inconsistent inputs.
key_works: Shuai Bai et al. (2025), [*Qwen2.5-VL Technical Report*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13923); Jin Xu et al. (2025), [*Qwen2.5-Omni Technical Report*, arXiv:2503.20215](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20215).

title: Thinker–Talker branch and streaming-audio consistency
subfield: Multimodal input, alignment, and output proofs
open: Can an end-to-end proof system bind a multimodal model's text generation, the hidden representations handed to its speech branch, the resulting audio tokens, and the final waveform decoding into a single state-transition proof? For ten minutes of continuous spoken output, the proof should be streamable in real time — with memory independent of the output horizon and the first certified audio available within two seconds after inference produces it.
status: Qwen2.5-Omni (Jin Xu et al., 2025, arXiv:2503.20215) introduces the Thinker–Talker architecture with a streaming speech decoder, but existing verification addresses only text correctness; no proof system yet covers the speech branch or streaming audio consistency.
solved_when: A single state-transition proof covers text, hidden representations passed to the speech branch, audio tokens, and waveform decoding, and over ten minutes of output the verifier's memory stays independent of the horizon while the first certified audio appears within two seconds after inference produces it.
why: Text correctness alone does not certify the speech branch, so users currently have no assurance that the spoken output follows the same approved computation as the displayed text.
key_works: Jin Xu et al. (2025), [*Qwen2.5-Omni Technical Report*, arXiv:2503.20215](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20215).

title: Residual-quantization neural audio-codec proofs
subfield: Multimodal input, alignment, and output proofs
open: Can a residual-quantization neural audio codec be accompanied by a succinct proof that the compressed tokens were produced and decoded correctly — covering residual-codebook selection, residual updates, the bandwidth-dependent number of codebooks, and causal decoding state — so that delivered audio is verifiably bound to its tokens?
status: EnCodec (Alexandre Défossez, Jade Copet, Gabriel Synnaeve, Yossi Adi, 2022, *High Fidelity Neural Audio Compression*, arXiv:2210.13438) establishes streaming neural compression with quantized latent representations; a complete residual-codec proof remains a proposed extension.
solved_when: For 60 seconds of 24-kHz audio, proof generation completes within 60 seconds and the final evidence is below 1 MB, with exact fixed-point conformance to the codec.
why: Without such proofs, audio-token integrity is incomplete: nothing binds the tokens, the codebooks, and the delivered PCM together, so downstream consumers cannot trust that decoded audio corresponds to what was compressed.
key_works: Alexandre Défossez, Jade Copet, Gabriel Synnaeve, Yossi Adi (2022), [*High Fidelity Neural Audio Compression*, arXiv:2210.13438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13438).

title: V-trace correction with authenticated behavior probabilities
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Can a zero-knowledge proof certify a full V-trace off-policy correction — binding the actor, target policy, value checkpoints, and terminal masks, and faithfully encoding V-trace's distinct clipped ratios and their products — even when the behavior policy's probabilities must themselves be authenticated? Formally, for \(0\le\bar c\le\min(1,\bar\rho)\), \(\bar\rho\le10\), discount at most 0.99, bounded rewards and values, and behavior probabilities at least \(2^{-24}\), the target error should stay below \(10^{-4}\) over 1,000 steps with linear proving work.
status: IMPALA (Lasse Espeholt et al., 2018, arXiv:1802.01561) establishes V-trace, and zkUCB (Xikun Jiang et al., 2024, arXiv:2404.12186) supplies a narrower bandit-verification result; the combined numerical and cryptographic target remains a proposed extension.
solved_when: A construction exists meeting all stated quantitative bounds: clipping parameters \(0\le\bar c\le\min(1,\bar\rho)\) with \(\bar\rho\le10\), discount at most 0.99, bounded rewards and values, behavior probabilities at least \(2^{-24}\), target error below \(10^{-4}\) over 1,000 steps, and linear proving work, while binding actor, target-policy, value checkpoints, and terminal masks.
why: Forged behavior probabilities can invalidate an otherwise correctly calculated off-policy update, so without authenticated probabilities a verifier cannot trust V-trace-based replay at all.
key_works: Lasse Espeholt et al. (2018), [*IMPALA*, arXiv:1802.01561](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.01561); Xikun Jiang et al. (2024), [*Privacy-Preserving UCB Decision Process Verification via zk-SNARKs*, arXiv:2404.12186](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.12186).

title: Private prioritized-replay normalization and priority refresh
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Can a replay provider prove, in zero knowledge, that each prioritized-replay draw is faithful to the committed buffer state and fresh unpredictable randomness — covering priority exponents, positive-priority or zero-total rules, normalized importance weights, and TD-error refreshes — without revealing which indices or priorities were involved?
status: Prioritized Experience Replay (Tom Schaul, John Quan, Ioannis Antonoglou, David Silver, 2016; preprint 2015, arXiv:1511.05952) specifies the sampling and correction algorithm; the private proof system described above is a further target, not an existing result.
solved_when: A private proof system handles buffers of \(10^7\) transitions with \(O(\log N)\) authenticated work per draw/update, proving sampling and correction against the committed state while hiding indices and priorities.
why: Correct cumulative arithmetic alone does not prevent a provider from choosing favorable samples, so verifiable replay arithmetic without sampling-faithfulness proofs leaves the training pipeline's data selection unaccountable.
key_works: Tom Schaul, John Quan, Ioannis Antonoglou, David Silver (2016; preprint 2015), [*Prioritized Experience Replay*, arXiv:1511.05952](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.05952).

title: Replay capacity and update-to-data ratio certificates
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Can a verifier, given a single ordered environment log, be convinced that a replay buffer's admission policy, FIFO eviction order, per-transition update counters, and reuse limits were all respected across a full training run? The target is to certify \(10^8\) insertions into a \(10^6\)-entry buffer at under 5% extra proof cost, even under concurrent inserts and samples.
status: Fedus et al. analyze replay capacity and replay ratio as consequential algorithmic controls in William Fedus et al. (2020), [*Revisiting Fundamentals of Experience Replay*, arXiv:2007.06700](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.06700), but their work does not supply these stateful ZK guarantees.
solved_when: A zkRL system produces, against one ordered environment log, checkable certificates of admission, FIFO eviction, update counters, and permitted transition reuse covering \(10^8\) insertions into a \(10^6\)-entry buffer, with less than 5% additional proof cost, and correctly handling concurrent inserts and samples.
why: Authenticity of individual samples says nothing about whether the claimed replay regime — capacity, eviction order, and update-to-data ratio — was actually followed, so verifiers can currently be shown honest-looking data from a noncompliant replay pipeline.
key_works: William Fedus et al. (2020), [*Revisiting Fundamentals of Experience Replay*, arXiv:2007.06700](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.06700).

title: Double-Q selection and target-network synchronization
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Can a ZK proof certify that Double DQN's action selection is computed with the online Q-network while evaluation uses the prescribed target checkpoint — including argmax ties and every scheduled target-network copy?
status: Double DQN (van Hasselt, Guez, Silver, 2016; preprint 2015, [arXiv:1509.06461](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.06461)) establishes the separate selection and evaluation roles; a matched stateful ZK implementation meeting the stated target was not established in the reviewed sources.
solved_when: A stateful ZK implementation proves the selection/evaluation split (with tie handling and all target copies) over \(10^6\) updates at less than 5% linkage overhead beyond the proofs of the two networks.
why: Substituting an online or stale target network silently changes the learning algorithm.
key_works: Hado van Hasselt, Arthur Guez, David Silver (2016; preprint 2015), [*Deep Reinforcement Learning with Double Q-learning*, arXiv:1509.06461](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.06461).

title: Soft actor-critic entropy and temperature-update proofs
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Can one full soft actor-critic training step — twin-critic targets, reparameterized actor sampling, the tanh change of variables, target-network averaging, and the automatic temperature update — be verified end-to-end as a single transition, rather than as separate unconnected pieces? Formally, the goal is a correctness proof covering the complete SAC update rule including its entropy and temperature machinery.
status: SAC (Haarnoja et al., 2018, arXiv:1812.05905) supplies the maximum-entropy algorithm and its temperature-tuning rule, and generic training proofs such as zkDL (Sun et al., 2023, arXiv:2307.16273) provide verifiable-training ingredients, but no existing work covers this complete, measured SAC workload.
solved_when: A single verified SAC transition exists, and the measured workload sustains \(10^5\) updates of 10M-parameter networks at less than 10× total runtime relative to the unverified baseline, including commitment costs.
why: Dropping the entropy correction or the evolving temperature state silently certifies a different objective than the one SAC actually optimizes, so any proof that skips these components is not a proof of SAC.
key_works: Tuomas Haarnoja et al. (2018), [*Soft Actor-Critic Algorithms and Applications*, arXiv:1812.05905](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.05905); Haochen Sun et al. (2023), [*zkDL*, arXiv:2307.16273](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.16273).

title: Mass-preserving categorical Bellman projection proofs
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Can we build a proof kernel that certifies a finite-precision categorical Bellman update — the support clipping, neighboring-bin interpolation, and terminal handling of C51 — while proving that probability mass is conserved up to the declared rounding? The target is correctness for \(10^6\) transitions with 51 atoms, at most \(10^{-6}\) \(L_1\) error per distribution, and verification work linear in the atom count.
status: Distributional RL establishes the categorical Bellman update (Marc G. Bellemare, Will Dabney, Rémi Munos (2017), [A Distributional Perspective on Reinforcement Learning, arXiv:1707.06887](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06887)), but its finite-precision proof kernel remains a proposed deliverable.
solved_when: A checkable proof certifies C51 support clipping, neighboring-bin interpolation, terminal handling, and probability-mass conservation under declared rounding for \(10^6\) transitions with 51 atoms, with at most \(10^{-6}\) \(L_1\) error per distribution and linear work in atom count.
why: Small probability-mass errors can accumulate through repeated distributional updates, so without such certification the zkRL distributional pipeline silently drifts off the simplex.
key_works: Marc G. Bellemare, Will Dabney, Rémi Munos (2017), [*A Distributional Perspective on Reinforcement Learning*, arXiv:1707.06887](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06887).

title: Quantile-Huber Bellman losses without quadratic witnesses
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Can the exact all-pairs quantile-Huber Bellman loss and its declared subgradient be proven succinctly, without ever materializing the \(K^2\) pairwise residuals that naive evaluation requires? Concretely, for \(K=1{,}024\) quantiles and batches of 4,096 transitions, is there a proof system whose auxiliary work and storage per transition is \(O(K\log K)\), handling sign and threshold ties exactly?
status: Quantile-regression RL (Dabney, Rowland, Bellemare, Munos, 2018, *Distributional Reinforcement Learning with Quantile Regression*, arXiv:1710.10044) supplies the objective; exploiting ordering and prefix statistics for a succinct private proof remains the proposed algorithmic frontier, with no known construction.
solved_when: A verifier-checkable proof certifies the exact all-pairs quantile-Huber loss and subgradient for \(K=1{,}024\) quantiles over batches of 4,096 transitions using \(O(K\log K)\) auxiliary work and storage per transition, including exact treatment of sign and threshold ties.
why: A quadratic auxiliary witness erases the benefit of compact distributional representations, so proving these losses succinctly is what makes private, verifiable distributional RL with replay actually practical.
key_works: Will Dabney, Mark Rowland, Marc G. Bellemare, Rémi Munos (2018), [*Distributional Reinforcement Learning with Quantile Regression*, arXiv:1710.10044](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.10044).

title: Recurrent replay burn-in and actor–learner staleness
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: How can a zkRL system prove that every recurrent hidden state used in replayed learning was obtained legitimately — that is, from an authorized learner checkpoint, with burn-in steps excluded from the training loss and actors at most a bounded version behind the learner — while scaling to 256 actors and \(10^6\) replayed sequences?
status: R2D2 (Kapturowski et al., 2019) studies recurrent-state staleness and representational drift, but its remedies do not themselves establish the proposed provenance certificate.
solved_when: A provenance certificate exists that certifies stored recurrent-state origins, learner checkpoint selection, exclusion of burn-in from the loss, and permitted actor version lag, handling 256 actors and \(10^6\) replayed sequences, and charging only executed burn-in and learning steps rather than complete episode replays.
why: Without such a certificate, a recurrent computation can start from an unauthorized or stale hidden state, making otherwise valid-looking training unverifiable.
key_works: Steven Kapturowski et al. (2019), [*Recurrent Experience Replay in Distributed Reinforcement Learning*](https://willdabney.com/publication/r2d2/).

title: Implicit-Q expectiles and logged-action restriction proofs
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Can an entire Implicit Q-Learning update — expectile regression on the value function, target bootstrapping, and clipped advantage-weighted policy extraction — be proven correct inside a single zkRL transition? In particular, the proof must enforce that every critic action query uses a committed logged action rather than an unseen one.
status: IQL avoids querying Q on unseen actions and extracts a policy through advantage-weighted cloning (Kostrikov, Nair, and Levine, 2022, arXiv:2110.06169); the corresponding private restricted-query proof remains to be built.
solved_when: A single-transition proof of the full IQL step exists that certifies the logged-action restriction on all critic queries, and runs for \(10^6\) transitions with a 100M-parameter policy at under 10× total overhead.
