why: IQL's correctness argument depends on never querying Q on unseen actions; without a proof of that restriction, the zkRL certificate does not actually validate the algorithm, only a data format.
key_works: Ilya Kostrikov, Ashvin Nair, Sergey Levine (2022), [*Offline Reinforcement Learning with Implicit Q-Learning*, arXiv:2110.06169](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.06169).

title: The joint constant-proof and linear-work multilinear PCS frontier
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Can a pairing-based multilinear polynomial commitment scheme achieve constant-size proofs and linear-time proving simultaneously? Formally, the goal is a scheme with at most \(2G_1+3\mathbb F\) opening elements, a two-term pairing check, \(O(N)\) field work, and at most \(N+o(N)\) MSM scalars, demonstrated at \(N\ge2^{20}\) with auxiliary commitments and setup counted.
status: Vela (Yuncong Zhang, 2026) reports a 200-byte opening but requires \(O(N\log N)\) field work; Carina achieves \(O(N)\) field work with a 452-byte opening. Neither supplies the requested combination. See Yuncong Zhang (2026), *Vela and Carina: Fast Pairing-Based Multilinear Polynomial Commitments from Reciprocal Polynomials*, ePrint 2026/1438.
solved_when: A pairing-based multilinear PCS is constructed meeting all targets: at most \(2G_1+3\mathbb F\) opening elements, a two-term pairing check, \(O(N)\) field work, at most \(N+o(N)\) MSM scalars, instantiated at \(N\ge2^{20}\), and accounting for auxiliary commitments and setup.
why: Proof size and prover time trade against each other — minimizing proof bytes alone can increase the dominant prover cost — so a scheme achieving both constants simultaneously would set the frontier for communication–computation tradeoffs in verifiable computation.
key_works: Yuncong Zhang (2026), [*Vela and Carina: Fast Pairing-Based Multilinear Polynomial Commitments from Reciprocal Polynomials*, ePrint 2026/1438](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1438).

title: QROM extraction for coordinate-wise lattice commitments
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Can Akita’s coordinate-wise, many-round extraction analysis be lifted to adversaries making quantum hash queries, while keeping its implemented folding and batching schedule intact? Formally, the goal is a justified knowledge-error bound with every reduction loss accounted for.
status: Akita’s analysis, as of September 2026, is in the classical random oracle model; its Section 14 explicitly leaves the QROM analysis as an open problem.
solved_when: A QROM extraction analysis for Akita’s coordinate-wise many-round extractor is established, preserving the implemented folding and batching schedule, with a justified knowledge-error bound of at most \(2^{-128}\) for \(q\le2^{64}\) and all reduction losses explicitly included.
why: Estimated lattice hardness of the underlying assumption and the quantum security of the complete proof transcript are currently separate guarantees; a QROM extractor is what welds them into a single end-to-end post-quantum security claim.
key_works: Quang Dao et al. (2026), [*Akita: A High-Performance Lattice-Based Polynomial Commitment Scheme*, Section 14](https://assets.layerzero.network/pdf/akita.pdf); Valerio Cini et al. (2024), [*Polynomial Commitments from Lattices: Post-Quantum Security, Fast Verification and Transparent Setup*, ePrint 2024/281](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/281).

title: Rigorous response-norm tails for optimized lattice folding
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Can the response-distribution assumptions underlying optimized later-fold schedules in lattice folding be proven, or replaced with rigorous bounds at quantified cost?
status: Akita explicitly identifies its optimized response-model premise as heuristic and requests either a proof or a quantified replacement; see Quang Dao et al. (2026), *Akita*, Section 14 and Appendix G.
solved_when: A proof (or rigorous replacement bounds) is given, with honest-prover rejection probability at most \(2^{-40}\) across \(10^6\) folds, while staying within 20% of the heuristic schedule's proof size and proving time.
why: Rare norm failures can undermine long-running proof-service reliability even when soundness remains intact.
key_works: Quang Dao et al. (2026), [*Akita*, Section 14 and Appendix G](https://assets.layerzero.network/pdf/akita.pdf).

title: Hiding lattice commitments without destroying sparse-input savings
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Can a sparse polynomial commitment scheme over lattices be made zero-knowledge without losing its sparsity advantage — that is, with commitment work scaling as \(O(s\operatorname{polylog}N)\) in the number \(s\) of nonzero entries? The scheme should remain efficient at low densities (at most \(1/256\)), incurring no more than 20% additional proof bytes and at most 2× prover work, and should come with simulation for batched openings and an explicit leakage analysis.
status: Akita (Quang Dao et al., 2026, [ePrint 2026/1983](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1983), [full paper](https://assets.layerzero.network/pdf/akita.pdf)) lists native zero knowledge as future work, and its sparse-commitment performance should not be treated as an existing hiding guarantee.
solved_when: A zero-knowledge sparse lattice PCS exists whose commitment work is \(O(s\operatorname{polylog}N)\), which at density at most \(1/256\) adds no more than 20% proof bytes and at most 2× prover work, with simulation for batched openings and an explicit account of leakage.
why: Dense masking can erase the sparse one-hot advantage that efficient lookup-heavy provers rely on, so without such a scheme zero knowledge and sparsity come at each other's expense.
key_works: Quang Dao et al. (2026), [*Akita*, ePrint 2026/1983](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1983), [full paper](https://assets.layerzero.network/pdf/akita.pdf).

title: Small-proof polylogarithmic verification for lattice commitments
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Can a lattice-based polynomial commitment scheme achieve transparent setup, polylogarithmic proof size and verification time, and quasilinear proving time all at once, with proofs of at most 16 KiB and verification within 5 ms on a single M4 Max CPU core at N = 2^30? The scheme should come with a justified 128-bit security target derived from standard Module-SIS, accounting for setup, norm growth, and security-dependent dimensions.
status: Polylogarithmic lattice verification already exists. Akita offers constant-root verification and reports 61–72 kB proofs in its benchmark regimes; the joint asymptotic and concrete target above is not established by these results.
solved_when: A transparent lattice polynomial commitment scheme is constructed with quasilinear proving, polylogarithmic proofs and verification, openings of at most 16 KiB, verification within 5 ms on one M4 Max CPU core at N = 2^30, and a rigorous 128-bit security reduction from standard Module-SIS that accounts for setup, norm growth, and security-dependent dimensions.
why: Large tensor proofs need small communication and fast verification simultaneously; without a scheme meeting both the asymptotic and concrete targets, such proofs remain impractical despite being theoretically succinct.
key_works: Valerio Cini et al. (2024), [*Polynomial Commitments from Lattices*, ePrint 2024/281](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/281); Quang Dao et al. (2026), [*Akita*, ePrint 2026/1983](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1983).

title: Fast pairing PCS knowledge soundness outside the algebraic group model
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Can the reciprocal-polynomial multilinear commitment schemes of Vela and Carina be proved knowledge-sound against fully general (non-algebraic) adversaries in the random oracle model, under a stated falsifiable assumption — or is there a genuine separation showing the algebraic group model is necessary for these schemes?
status: Vela/Carina (Yuncong Zhang, 2026, [Vela and Carina](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1438)) establishes its analysis in the algebraic group model plus ROM. Lipmaa's 2025 result ([Plonk is Simulation Extractable in ROM Under Falsifiable Assumptions](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1759)) removes the AGM but in a different setting, making this a scheme-specific extension rather than a direct corollary.
solved_when: A proof (or separation) exists for the commitment and opening algorithms exactly as specified, with a justified total knowledge-soundness error of at most \(2^{-128}\) for \(N=2^{30}\).
why: The extractability assumptions currently underpinning these schemes propagate directly into downstream claims about knowledge of hidden weights and witnesses, so removing the algebraic group model would place those claims on falsifiable foundations.
key_works: Yuncong Zhang (2026), [*Vela and Carina*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1438); Helger Lipmaa (2025), [*Plonk is Simulation Extractable in ROM Under Falsifiable Assumptions*, ePrint 2025/1759](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1759).

title: Multipoint multilinear opening complexity after one commitment
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: After committing once to a multilinear polynomial in \(N\) variables at \(O(N)\) cost, how efficiently can a prover answer \(k\) adversarially chosen evaluation queries at distinct points? Is total work \(O(N+k\operatorname{polylog}N)\) achievable for \(k\le\sqrt N\) with polylogarithmic proof size, or is there a matching lower bound forcing more work?
status: Samaritan (Ganesh, Patranabis, Singh, 2025, ePrint 2025/419) achieves \(O(N+k\sqrt N)\) cryptographic work in its batched regime, leaving the stronger amortization target unresolved.
solved_when: Either a scheme achieves \(O(N+k\operatorname{polylog}N)\) total work for \(k\le\sqrt N\) multilinear openings after one \(O(N)\) commitment, with polylogarithmic proof size, or a lower bound matching this target (ruling out such amortization) is established.
why: Many operator checks in verifiable ML open the same weight or activation polynomial at many different points, so the cost of repeated openings directly determines whether such proofs stay practical.
key_works: Chaya Ganesh, Sikhar Patranabis, Nitin Singh (2025), [*Samaritan: Linear-time Prover SNARK from New Multilinear Polynomial Commitments*, ePrint 2025/419](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/419).

title: Public-parameter lower bounds for bivariate Lagrange commitments
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Are \(O(m+n)\) public parameters necessary for algebraic pairing-based commitments to arbitrary bidegree-\((m,n)\) polynomials, or can the setup be made smaller? Formally, either exhibit an \(o(m+n)\)-size setup supporting \(O(mn)\) commitment and \(O(m+n)\) opening work, or prove a lower bound that counts all preprocessing advice.
status: GAPP's bivariate Lagrange-basis commitment (Chaya Ganesh et al., 2026, *GAPP: Generic Aggregation of Polynomial Protocols*, ePrint 2024/1685) achieves \(O(m+n)\) public parameters and opening cryptographic operations; whether this is optimal or can be strictly improved remains open.
solved_when: Either a construction with \(o(m+n)\) public parameters (maintaining \(O(mn)\) commitment size and \(O(m+n)\) opening operations) is given, or a lower bound on preprocessing advice rules out such a construction.
why: Large reusable setup data can undermine otherwise compact proof aggregation, so knowing whether \(O(m+n)\) is optimal determines whether the apparent succinctness of these commitments is genuine.
key_works: Chaya Ganesh et al. (2026), [*GAPP: Generic Aggregation of Polynomial Protocols*, ePrint 2024/1685](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1685).

title: Tight epoch–query tradeoffs for reused numerical proof queries
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: How tightly can a verifier's reused numerical proof queries be bounded when the statement is encoded as matrix products or lookup traces, while still leaking only accept/reject? The goal is to pin down the epoch–query tradeoff within a constant factor for \(r\in\{1,2,4,16,256\}\), \(N=2^{20}\) through \(2^{40}\), and error \(2^{-128}\).
status: *Query-Reusable Proof Systems* (Ishai, Kushilevitz, Narayanan, Ostrovsky, Shah, 2025) gives nearly tight general tradeoffs and limitations on unrestricted statistical reuse; structured numerical languages may permit sharper special cases.
solved_when: The epoch–query tradeoff for these structured encodings is determined within a constant factor over the stated parameter ranges: reuse count \(r\in\{1,2,4,16,256\}\), input size \(N=2^{20}\) to \(2^{40}\), and soundness error \(2^{-128}\), with leakage limited to accept/reject bits.
why: Reusing hidden verifier tests across many receipts creates an adaptive-feedback channel through which a prover can learn the secret tests; tight tradeoffs for structured numerical encodings show exactly when such reuse remains sound.
key_works: Yuval Ishai, Eyal Kushilevitz, Varun Narayanan, Rafail Ostrovsky, Akash Shah (2025), [*Query-Reusable Proof Systems*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-91134-7_12).

title: Concrete computational query reuse for a fixed model verifier
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Can one build a designated-verifier numerical proof system that safely reuses hidden query positions across \(10^6\) adaptive proofs, including malformed ones, so that verifier feedback never enables tailored later forgeries?
status: Positive query-reuse constructions exist when soundness or ZK is computational. The proposed numerical service benchmarks are additional. Key work: Yuval Ishai et al. (2025), [*Query-Reusable Proof Systems*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-91134-7_12).
solved_when: A working implementation reuses hidden query positions across \(10^6\) adaptive proofs (including malformed ones) with less than 1 MiB verifier state and 10 ms online verification at \(N=2^{20}\), under explicit computational assumptions.
why: A customer can amortize verification setup only if feedback does not enable tailored later forgeries; this makes repeated verification of a fixed model practical.
key_works: Yuval Ishai et al. (2025), [*Query-Reusable Proof Systems*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-91134-7_12).

title: Worst-case refresh cost for private authenticated numerical RAM
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Can we build a private authenticated RAM that serves a huge mutable store with hard worst-case guarantees on refresh cost rather than amortized ones? Concretely, the target is a system for \(2^{30}\) 64-bit words handling at most \(10^4\) application probes per request and at most \(2^{20}\) extra refresh operations on any single request, including at epoch boundaries.
status: Ishai, Ostrovsky and Shah (2025), [*Zero-Knowledge RAM: Doubly Efficient and Black-Box*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-91134-7_13), already support ZK RAM updates using black-box symmetric primitives; concrete worst-case refresh and latency bounds remain the application target.
solved_when: A construction achieves \(2^{30}\) 64-bit words of storage, at most \(10^4\) application probes per request, at most \(2^{20}\) extra refresh operations on any request (including epoch boundaries), p99 refresh slowdown below 2×, and is validated by simulation over \(10^6\) adaptive requests.
why: Amortized bounds can conceal unacceptable pauses in mutable embedding and optimizer stores, so worst-case refresh control is what makes such systems usable in practice.
key_works: Yuval Ishai, Rafail Ostrovsky, Akash Shah (2025), [*Zero-Knowledge RAM: Doubly Efficient and Black-Box*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-91134-7_13).

title: CRS compression using only collision-resistant hashing
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Can the CRS of a succinct proof system be compressed using nothing beyond collision-resistant hashing, without delegating RAM computation? More precisely, can the CRS-shortening step of succinctness boosting be made to rely only on CRHFs in addition to the starting proof system, achieving CRS size poly(λ, n, log T) for T-step numerical programs?
status: Cheng–Goyal (2025) [*Boosting SNARKs and Rate-1 Barrier in Arguments of Knowledge*](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.56) explicitly ask whether RAM delegation in this step can be eliminated or replaced by CRHFs; the problem remains open.
solved_when: A construction achieves CRS size poly(λ, n, log T) for T-step numerical programs whose CRS-compression step uses only collision-resistant hash families, with efficient RAM delegation removed from that step.
why: Large setup data and stronger assumptions can dominate deployments where the model changes frequently, so removing them makes succinct proofs practical for such settings.
key_works: Jiaqi Cheng, Rishab Goyal (2025), [*Boosting SNARKs and Rate-1 Barrier in Arguments of Knowledge*](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.56).

title: Additive-overhead complexity-preserving proof generation
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Can a generic computation of time \(T\) and space \(S\) be certified with only additive overhead — prover time \(T+\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,\log T)\) and space \(S+\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,\log T)\) — rather than the usual multiplicative blowup? A satisfactory answer must fix a RAM model and charge randomness generation, setup, and output writing explicitly.
status: Replacing fixed multiplicative overhead with fixed additive overhead is a published open question posed by Cheng–Goyal (2025) in *Boosting SNARKs and Rate-1 Barrier in Arguments of Knowledge* (https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.56); no construction or barrier is known.
solved_when: A construction (or a barrier) exists for generic succinctness boosting in which prover time is \(T+\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,\log T)\) and prover space is \(S+\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,\log T)\), with the RAM model and all costs — randomness generation, setup, and output writing — explicitly specified and charged.
why: It asks whether the asymptotic cost of certification can approach the cost of execution itself, closing the gap between proving a computation and merely running it.
key_works: Jiaqi Cheng, Rishab Goyal (2025), [*Boosting SNARKs and Rate-1 Barrier in Arguments of Knowledge*](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.56).

title: Polynomial-depth IVC security in the ordinary ROM
subfield: Recursive knowledge and adaptive simulation
open: Can knowledge soundness of polynomial-depth, two-curve numerical IVC be established in the ordinary random oracle model, without recourse to an open-and-sign oracle or algebraic representations of the adversary? The extractor should run in polynomial time in the total trace length and the inverse acceptance probability, covering recursion depths up to \(10^6\) proof steps.
status: Maller, Mohnblatt and Zapico (2025, *IVC in the Open-and-sign Random Oracle Model*, ePrint 2025/1663) prove polynomial-depth security in the open-and-sign ROM, an explicitly stronger idealization than the ordinary ROM. Transferring the guarantee to the ordinary ROM is the remaining question.
solved_when: A proof of knowledge soundness for polynomial-depth, two-curve numerical IVC in the ordinary ROM is given, with extraction time polynomial in the total trace length and the inverse acceptance probability, valid for executions of \(10^6\) proof steps, and using neither an open-and-sign oracle nor adversary algebraic representations.
why: A justified extraction theorem across the entire recursion is what makes long-execution certificates from IVC trustworthy; without it, the soundness of deeply recursive proofs rests on an unjustified idealization.
key_works: Mary Maller, Nicolas Mohnblatt, Arantxa Zapico (2025), [*IVC in the Open-and-sign Random Oracle Model*, ePrint 2025/1663](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1663).

title: Recursive simulation extractability across evolving setup histories
subfield: Recursive knowledge and adaptive simulation
open: Can proof-carrying data achieve simulation extractability when the structured reference string itself evolves under adversarial, correlated updates — including merging branches proven under different reachable setups? Formally, the goal is a single explicit simulator/extractor analysis covering a recursive PCD system over evolving setup histories, robust up to \(10^4\) adversarial SRS updates and a \(10^6\)-node DAG, with total failure probability at most \(2^{-128}\).
status: Positive results now exist separately for PCD-specific simulation extractability (Behzad Abdolmaleki et al., 2026; preprint 2025, *On the Simulation-Extractability of Proof-Carrying Data*, ePrint 2025/2037) and for stronger updatable simulation-extractability definitions (Hamidreza Khoshakhlagh 2026, *Revisiting Simulation Extractability in the Updatable Setting*, ePrint 2025/2117); their joint adaptive-recursion setting remains the proposed extension.
solved_when: A construction and proof exist that combine PCD simulation extractability with adversarially updated, correlated SRS histories (including merges of branches under different reachable setups), with one unified simulator/extractor analysis handling at least \(10^4\) updates and \(10^6\)-node DAGs with total failure probability at most \(2^{-128}\).
why: Long-lived proof histories routinely outlive the setups they were created under, crossing setup updates and organizational boundaries; without a security definition and proof for this regime, composability of such histories rests on unverified assumptions.
key_works: Behzad Abdolmaleki et al. (2026; preprint 2025), [*On the Simulation-Extractability of Proof-Carrying Data*, ePrint 2025/2037](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/2037); Hamidreza Khoshakhlagh (2026), [*Revisiting Simulation Extractability in the Updatable Setting*, ePrint 2025/2117](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/2117).

title: Efficient adaptive-corruption simulation of streaming proof state
subfield: Recursive knowledge and adaptive simulation
open: Can a prover maintain a streaming zero-knowledge proof across a long computation while remaining simulatable against an adversary who adaptively corrupts its memory up to \(10^6\) times, with the simulation conditioned only on explicitly exposed application state and outputs?
status: Afshar and Goyal (2025, *Verifiable Streaming Computation and Step-by-Step Zero-Knowledge*, ePrint 2025/251) introduce verifiable streaming computation and step-by-step ZK, including internal-state simulation; the concrete multiple-snapshot numerical target above extends that foundation.
solved_when: A construction achieves simulatability under \(10^6\) adaptively chosen snapshot corruptions, with at most 2× prover time overhead and \(O(S+\operatorname{polylog}T)\) live storage, in a precisely specified erasure and corruption model.
why: Final-transcript zero knowledge says nothing about what an attacker learns from a live proof worker mid-computation; this closes that gap for persistent, memory-resident proving systems.
key_works: Abtin Afshar, Rishab Goyal (2025), [*Verifiable Streaming Computation and Step-by-Step Zero-Knowledge*, ePrint 2025/251](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/251).

title: Private stateless handoff of recursive numerical proofs
subfield: Recursive knowledge and adaptive simulation
open: Can a recursive proving task be handed off between independent workers so that nothing leaks beyond an explicitly declared public state? Formally, the handoff should achieve polylogarithmic handoff bytes and persistent proof state — excluding the next worker's fresh local witness — at most 2× per-step cost on \(2^{24}\)-constraint steps.
status: Holography accumulation (Paslis, Ràfols, Zacharakis, 2026, [Proof-Carrying Data via Holography Accumulation, ePrint 2026/538](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/538)) supplies stateless recursion for the relevant SNARK classes, but private handoff with the stated concrete costs remains a further target.
solved_when: A private stateless handoff scheme exists for the relevant SNARK classes with polylogarithmic handoff bytes and persistent proof state (excluding the next worker's fresh local witness) and per-step overhead at most 2× on \(2^{24}\)-constraint steps.
why: Without it, migrating a proving job between workers forces disclosure of the entire private proof history; with it, worker migration discloses only the declared public state.
key_works: Nikitas Paslis, Carla Ràfols, Alexandros Zacharakis (2026), [*Proof-Carrying Data via Holography Accumulation*, ePrint 2026/538](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/538).

title: From binding commitments to computationally unique witnesses
subfield: Recursive knowledge and adaptive simulation
open: Can SNARKs with adaptive soundness be built for computations whose witnesses are unique only computationally — fixed by the binding property of commitments rather than by the relation itself? In particular, can UP-style techniques be extended to deterministic numerical executions with committed hidden inputs, achieving proof and verification complexity polynomial in the security parameter and log T under falsifiable standard-model assumptions, or is there a fundamental barrier?
status: Mathialagan, Peters and Vaikuntanathan (2024, *Adaptively Sound Zero-Knowledge SNARKs for UP*, ePrint 2024/227) handle UP's literal information-theoretic witness uniqueness in a reusable designated-verifier model. Computational binding does not make every committed-input relation information-theoretically unambiguous, leaving the computational-uniqueness case open.
solved_when: A construction with proof and verification complexity polynomial in λ and log T for committed-input deterministic executions under falsifiable standard-model assumptions is given, or a formal barrier to such constructions is established.
why: "Deterministic execution" and "unique NP witness" are genuinely different properties when inputs remain hidden, so existing UP techniques do not automatically transfer; settling this determines whether commitment-based hiding of inputs is compatible with adaptively sound succinct proofs.
key_works: Surya Mathialagan, Spencer Peters, Vinod Vaikuntanathan (2024), [*Adaptively Sound Zero-Knowledge SNARKs for UP*, ePrint 2024/227](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/227).

title: Complete-candidate cross-encoder reranking
subfield: Structured, learned, and distributed retrieval proofs
open: Can a retrieval system prove that every candidate passage retrieved for a query was actually scored by the cross-encoder and ranked, with nothing quietly dropped? Concretely, bind the retrieved candidate multiset to each query–passage encoding, cross-encoder score, calibration step, and final rank, proving each required candidate was scored exactly once.
status: BERT passage reranking (Nogueira and Cho, 2019, *Passage Re-ranking with BERT*, arXiv:1901.04085) defines the ordinary reranking stage, and inference and retrieval proofs supply separate ingredients; what remains missing is candidate completeness and the linkage between them. ZKTorch (Chen et al., 2025, arXiv:2507.07031) is relevant machinery.
solved_when: A construction demonstrates complete-candidate linkage for a workload of 1,000 passages of 512 tokens each, completing in less than 30 seconds on eight GPUs with below 5% bookkeeping overhead.
why: Without candidate completeness and linkage, a service can selectively avoid scoring inconvenient candidates while still showing correct retrieval, silently skewing the final ranking.
key_works: Rodrigo Nogueira, Kyunghyun Cho (2019), [*Passage Re-ranking with BERT*, arXiv:1901.04085](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.04085); Bing-Jyue Chen et al. (2025), [*ZKTorch*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07031).

title: HNSW graph-construction and neighbor-pruning lineage
subfield: Structured, learned, and distributed retrieval proofs
open: Can a full HNSW index be proven correct at construction time, so that the published index is certified rather than merely claimed? Formally, produce a verifiable proof of the entire construction lineage — insertion of every committed vector, level randomness, insertion order, neighbor selection, reciprocal-edge updates, and pruning.
status: Atlas (Nikolay Avramov et al. (2026), arXiv:2609.11841) proves queries over a committed HNSW index but explicitly treats index construction and well-formedness as orthogonal, leaving the construction lineage unproven. The underlying structure is from Yu. A. Malkov, D. A. Yashunin (2016), arXiv:1603.09320.
solved_when: Construction is proven for all \(10^6\) vectors with upper-layer degree 32, completing the proof within 24 hours on a single server, with final evidence below 1 MB.
why: Faithful search over a maliciously constructed graph can systematically conceal relevant items, so a query-time proof alone cannot rule out a poisoned index.
key_works: Yu. A. Malkov, D. A. Yashunin (2016), [*Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs*, arXiv:1603.09320](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320); Nikolay Avramov et al. (2026), [*Atlas*, arXiv:2609.11841](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11841).

title: HNSW termination proofs without a fixed truncation budget
subfield: Structured, learned, and distributed retrieval proofs
open: Can the original HNSW termination condition and the full evolution of the frontier and visited set be proven correct while charging verification work only to the traversal actually realized, rather than to a budget fixed in advance? Formally, produce a termination-and-execution proof for the untruncated algorithm that is exact for a pinned implementation and output-sensitive in work.
status: Atlas (Nikolay Avramov et al., 2026, *Atlas: Efficient Verifiable Semantic Search*, arXiv:2609.11841) instead uses fixed step budgets and studies the recall loss truncation causes; untruncated adaptive execution remains distinct from, and unaddressed by, exact global-neighbor certification.
solved_when: Across 10,000 queries on \(10^8\) vectors, the proof system achieves exact agreement with the pinned reference implementation, with median work within 1.5× and p99 work within 2× that of an ideally sized circuit.
why: Tail queries should not silently lose retrieval quality because termination was truncated by a budget tuned for typical queries.
key_works: Nikolay Avramov et al. (2026), [*Atlas: Efficient Verifiable Semantic Search*, arXiv:2609.11841](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11841).

title: PQ and OPQ codebook-training certificates
subfield: Structured, learned, and distributed retrieval proofs
open: Can a product-quantization index prove that its own codebooks were trained honestly — covering training-data selection, centroid assignments and updates, empty-cluster handling, OPQ rotation steps, and the final encoding — rather than merely that lookups were executed against whatever tables were supplied? Formally, the target is to certify the full training pipeline for \(10^7\) training vectors, 32 subquantizers, 256 codewords, and 20 iterations in under 5× plaintext index-training time, with a proved rotation tolerance.
status: OPQ (Ge, He, Ke, Sun 2013) and the Faiss library (Douze et al., 2024, arXiv:2401.08281) supply the training procedures, and V3DB proves correct execution of IVF-PQ queries; however, correct index training is a different statement and remains unproven.
solved_when: A certificate exists for all training stages — data selection, assignments, centroid updates, empty clusters, OPQ rotations, and final codes — running below 5× plaintext index-training time at the stated scale (\(10^7\) vectors, 32 subquantizers, 256 codewords, 20 iterations), with a proved tolerance for the rotations.
why: An authentic query-execution transcript is meaningless if the underlying compression tables were trained incorrectly or adversarially, since verifiable lookups against bad codebooks still return wrong nearest-neighbor results.
key_works: Tiezheng Ge, Kaiming He, Qifa Ke, Jian Sun (2013), [*Optimized Product Quantization for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search*](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/optimized-product-quantization-for-approximate-nearest-neighbor-search/); Matthijs Douze et al. (2024), [*The Faiss library*, arXiv:2401.08281](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08281).

title: Late-interaction MaxSim and residual-decoding proofs
subfield: Structured, learned, and distributed retrieval proofs
open: Can we build a proof system that certifies late-interaction retrieval scoring — verifying both the residual decompression of stored embeddings and the per-query-token maximum similarity over every declared document-token embedding, including padding and boundary tokens — at practical cost?
status: ColBERTv2 (Keshav Santhanam et al., 2022, [arXiv:2112.01488](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.01488)) specifies compressed multi-vector late interaction, but single-vector ANN proof statements do not cover document-internal MaxSim reductions.
solved_when: A verifiable proof of residual decompression and each query-token MaxSim reduction over all declared document tokens runs, for 32 query tokens, 1,000 documents, and 256 tokens per document, in under five seconds, with witness memory below 2× the compressed-index size.
why: Without such proofs, a malicious or buggy server can substitute embeddings or omit a maximizing token to manipulate relevance scores undetected, undermining trust in retrieved results.
key_works: Keshav Santhanam et al. (2022), [*ColBERTv2: Effective and Efficient Retrieval via Lightweight Late Interaction*, arXiv:2112.01488](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.01488).

title: Shard-map-complete distributed retrieval merges
subfield: Structured, learned, and distributed retrieval proofs
open: Can a distributed retrieval system prove, at a single corpus epoch, that every required shard actually participated in a query answer — or else authenticate that it was safely excluded — before deduplication and merging are performed? Formally, for a fan-out over 256 shards with \(k=20\), produce shard-map-complete aggregation evidence in under one second and final evidence under 1 MB.
status: Vector-search systems and committed-snapshot proofs supply the local components, but complete fan-out and cross-shard epoch consistency still require additional evidence (Douze et al. 2024, *The Faiss library*, arXiv:2401.08281; Qio et al. 2026, *V3DB*, arXiv:2603.03065).
solved_when: A construction exists that, for 256 shards and \(k=20\), proves participation of every required shard at one corpus epoch (or authenticated safe exclusion) prior to deduplication and merging, with aggregation proving below one second and final evidence below 1 MB.
why: Every returned shard proof can be individually valid while an entire required shard is silently missing from the merge.
key_works: Matthijs Douze et al. (2024), [*The Faiss library*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08281); Zipeng Qiu et al. (2026), [*V3DB*, arXiv:2603.03065](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03065).

title: GraphRAG community and summary-dependency certificates
subfield: Structured, learned, and distributed retrieval proofs
open: Can a GraphRAG pipeline produce verifiable certificates for its retrieval structure — covering extraction outputs, partition membership, community-summary inputs, and the map/reduce dependency of answers on summaries? Formally, under a pinned pipeline, prove that answers depend only on attested summaries and that each summary depends only on attested community inputs.
status: GraphRAG (Darren Edge et al. (2024), [*From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization*, arXiv:2404.16130](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130)) constructs entity graphs and community summaries, but proving derivation does not make extracted relations or summaries factually correct — no such certificate system exists yet.
solved_when: For a corpus of \(10^6\) chunks and three community levels, the certificate system adds less than 10% extra provenance storage, and updates after corpus changes touch only affected summaries and their ancestors.
why: Missing communities or incomplete summary inputs can silently bias global answers, so certificates make such corruption detectable rather than invisible.
key_works: Darren Edge et al. (2024), [*From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization*, arXiv:2404.16130](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130).

title: Learned-sparse expansion and inverted-index pruning proofs
subfield: Structured, learned, and distributed retrieval proofs
open: Can a succinct proof system certify that a learned-sparse retrieval pipeline — SPLADE-style learned expansion weights, log saturation, pooling, and thresholding — was executed faithfully, including every pruning bound (e.g., WAND/MaxScore-style skips) used to avoid visiting postings? In particular, can the full declared sparse algorithm be proven correct on a corpus of \(10^7\) passages with queries of at most 256 nonzero terms?
status: SPLADE (Thibault Formal, Benjamin Piwowarski, Stéphane Clinchant, 2021, [arXiv:2107.05720](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.05720)) supplies the learned-sparse retrieval semantics, whose statements differ from both fixed BM25 statistics and dense-vector ANN formulations; no proofs of the expansion, saturation, pooling, or pruning components are known.
solved_when: For \(10^7\) passages and at most 256 nonzero query terms, the prover certifies top-20 equality with the declared sparse algorithm, with proof work at most 2× the number of postings actually visited.
why: Learned term weights make the verification obligations qualitatively harder than for BM25 or dense ANN: every model-derived expansion weight and every pruning decision becomes an additional claim that must be proven, so without such proofs learned-sparse retrieval cannot be used where computation must be audited.
key_works: Thibault Formal, Benjamin Piwowarski, Stéphane Clinchant (2021), [*SPLADE: Sparse Lexical and Expansion Model for First Stage Ranking*, arXiv:2107.05720](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.05720).

title: Work overhead required for white-box-resistant Fiat–Shamir
subfield: Fiat–Shamir and concrete-hash foundations
open: How much extra work must a prover do to make Fiat–Shamir resistance to white-box (diagonalization) attacks practical? More precisely, determine the minimum additional prover work required for XFS-style resistance to diagonalization, and whether comparable protection can avoid proof-of-work altogether.
status: Arnon and Yogev's XFS construction, published at CRYPTO 2025, provides security evidence in a relativized random-oracle model, but does not establish security for arbitrary concrete hashes.
solved_when: The minimum additional prover overhead for XFS-style diagonalization resistance is determined, meeting the target of at most 5% additional proving and verification work under the stated relativized-oracle model, and it is established whether comparable protection can avoid proof-of-work.
why: A defensive transform must remain affordable when applied to every inference or training receipt.
key_works: Gal Arnon, Eylon Yogev (2025), [*Towards a White-Box Secure Fiat-Shamir Transformation*, ePrint 2025/329](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/329).

title: Optimal challenge independence for shared polynomial proof graphs
subfield: Fiat–Shamir and concrete-hash foundations
open: Which dependency graphs allow a collection of polynomial checks to safely share random challenges, rather than drawing fresh randomness for each? Formally, characterize when $2^{20}$ degree-at-most-8 checks arranged in $M$ independent stages can be verified using $O(\lambda + \log M)$ random bits per stage with total error at most $2^{-128}$, or prove that more randomness is inherently required.
status: The GAPP framework of Chaya Ganesh, Sikhar Patranabis, Shubh Prakash, and Nitin Singh (2026; preprint 2024) provides the algebraic packing and aggregation machinery, but optimal randomness use across dependent numerical checks remains a further open question.
solved_when: A characterization is given of the dependency graphs for which $2^{20}$ degree-at-most-8 polynomial checks can share challenges at $O(\lambda + \log M)$ random bits per independent stage with total error at most $2^{-128}$, or a lower bound is proven showing a larger randomness requirement for some class of graphs.
why: Knowing exactly when challenge reuse is legal governs both the efficiency of batching many checks and the soundness of composing tensor-style proofs built from them.
key_works: Chaya Ganesh, Sikhar Patranabis, Shubh Prakash, Nitin Singh (2026; preprint 2024), [*GAPP: Generic Aggregation of Polynomial Protocols*, ePrint 2024/1685](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1685).

title: PCS verifier lower bounds with reusable cryptographic preprocessing
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Can we prove verifier communication lower bounds for Bulletproofs-style inner-product-argument polynomial commitments when the verifier is allowed to reuse cryptographic preprocessing across many evaluations? Concretely, with transparent generators, no verifier trapdoor, and \(S\) bits of reusable preprocessing, determine an online verification tradeoff such as \(V=\Omega(N/S)\), including the regimes \(S=N^\alpha\) for \(\alpha\in\{0,1/4,1/2\}\).
status: Bhadauria et al. (2025, ePrint 2025/1698) give communication-core bounds of \(\Omega(\sqrt N)\), \(\Omega(N)\), and \(\Omega(\log N)\) for Hyrax, Bulletproofs, and Dory respectively; these are not unconditional bounds for every polynomial commitment scheme. No lower bounds are known for the setting with \(S\) bits of reusable cryptographic preprocessing.
solved_when: A proof (in an explicitly defined model covering Bulletproofs-style discrete-log IPA commitments with transparent generators and no verifier trapdoor) establishes an online verification lower bound of the form \(V=\Omega(N/S)\) — or another justified tradeoff — for the stated preprocessing regimes \(S=N^\alpha\), \(\alpha\in\{0,1/4,1/2\}\).
why: When a PCS verifier is used repeatedly, the standard one-shot accounting no longer reflects what can be shifted into reusable precomputation, so existing lower bounds may overstate true costs; a proof clarifies what Bulletproofs-style systems must actually pay online.
key_works: Rishabh Bhadauria, Alexander R. Block, Prantar Ghosh, Justin Thaler (2025), [*SNARK Lower Bounds via Communication Complexity*, ePrint 2025/1698](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1698).

title: Controlled malleability for richer tensor commitment transformations
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Which public transformations of tensor commitments — permutations, reshapes, slices, and rank-r maps — can be made safely malleable, in the sense that anyone can update both the commitment and its proof under the transformation without breaking soundness? Formally, characterize a family of permitted transformations, with descriptors that are either succinct or preprocessed into commitments, such that verifiers do \(O(r\operatorname{polylog}N)\) additional work for rank-\(r\) maps with \(r\le64\), descriptor access is properly accounted for, and transformations outside the declared family are rejected.
status: Faonio and Russo ([*Sumcheck-based zkSNARKs are Non-Malleable*, ePrint 2026/335](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/335), 2026) show that controlled linear malleability suffices for non-malleable sumcheck SNARKs even when the underlying polynomial commitment scheme lacks simulation extractability; extending this to richer tensor transformations remains unanalyzed.
solved_when: A characterization exists (or, for a construction, a scheme is given) of safe public transformations covering permutations, reshapes, slices, and rank-\(r\) maps for \(r\le64\), with \(O(r\operatorname{polylog}N)\) additional verifier work, succinct transformation descriptions or preprocessed descriptor commitments, an accounting of descriptor access, and rejection of transformations outside the declared family.
why: Tensor-based proof systems intentionally apply algebraic transformations to committed data, so a commitment scheme must let exactly the permitted algebra go through while preventing proof substitution and other malleability attacks; without such control, transformations and forgeries become indistinguishable.
key_works: Antonio Faonio, Luigi Russo (2026), [*Sumcheck-based zkSNARKs are Non-Malleable*, ePrint 2026/335](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/335).

title: Trapdoorless zero knowledge for standalone linearization gadgets
subfield: Recursive knowledge and adaptive simulation
open: Can commit-and-prove linearization gadgets be given their own local zero-knowledge property without relying on trapdoors, or is there an unavoidable overhead bound? The target is a locally simulatable replacement with at most two additional commitments and at most 10% additional prover arithmetic, whose security composes with sumcheck and lookup relations — or a proof that this cannot be done.
status: Lipmaa (2025, *Plonk is Simulation Extractable in ROM Under Falsifiable Assumptions*, ePrint 2025/1759) proves whole-protocol Plonk simulation extractability while showing that several standalone gadgets lack trapdoorless zero knowledge, so global security does not automatically supply the desired local contract.
solved_when: A locally simulatable trapdoorless replacement for the gadget family is constructed meeting the quantitative budgets (at most two extra commitments, at most 10% extra prover arithmetic, security composing with sumcheck and lookup relations), or a lower bound proving some minimum overhead is established.
why: Modular proof libraries require security interfaces that match how their components are actually reused; without local guarantees, global protocol security cannot be safely lifted to standalone gadget contracts.
key_works: Helger Lipmaa (2025), [*Plonk is Simulation Extractable in ROM Under Falsifiable Assumptions*, ePrint 2025/1759](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1759).

title: Access-pattern lower bounds for offline and limited-lookahead AI proving
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: How much bandwidth overhead is unavoidable when a prover gets to see some of the future before committing to its memory traffic? Formally, characterize the bandwidth–privacy frontier for proving with lookahead B, separating the regimes B=1, B=log N, and B=N^α, and determine in which of them sublogarithmic overhead is achievable with only polylogarithmic private client storage.
status: Online ORAM has logarithmic bandwidth lower bounds, including strengthened models that hide operation boundaries (Hubáček, Koucký, Král, Slívová, 2019, [Stronger Lower Bounds for Online ORAM, arXiv:1903.03385](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.03385)). Those results do not automatically cover an already recorded tensor trace.
solved_when: A theorem (or matching lower and upper bounds) pins down, for each of B=1, B=log N, and B=N^α, whether sublogarithmic bandwidth overhead is possible with polylogarithmic private client storage, and separates the regimes where it is not.
why: Offline proving may be able to escape the known online ORAM barriers, but that escape requires a genuinely different theorem; settling this determines whether limited-lookahead AI provers can beat logarithmic overhead.
key_works: Pavel Hubáček, Michal Koucký, Karel Král, Veronika Slívová (2019), [*Stronger Lower Bounds for Online ORAM*, arXiv:1903.03385](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.03385).

title: Succinctness boosting without full witness extraction
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Can mildly succinct SNARGs that lack full knowledge soundness be compressed into fully succinct ones? Concretely, compress proofs of length \(m/\lambda+\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,n)\) down to \(\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,n,\log m)\) under an explicitly stated weak-extraction premise.
status: Cheng–Goyal explicitly leave boosting without, or with very weak, extractability open (Jiaqi Cheng, Rishab Goyal (2025), *Boosting SNARKs and Rate-1 Barrier in Arguments of Knowledge*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.56).
solved_when: A construction achieves \(\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,n,\log m)\)-length proofs starting from proofs of length \(m/\lambda+\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,n)\), with the weak-extraction premise under which it is proven made explicit.
why: Cheap validity checks may lack the extractors required by existing compression methods, so such a construction would extend succinctness boosting to settings currently out of reach.
key_works: Jiaqi Cheng, Rishab Goyal (2025), [*Boosting SNARKs and Rate-1 Barrier in Arguments of Knowledge*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.56](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.56).

title: Succinctness boosting from nonadaptive inner soundness
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Can mildly succinct proofs that are only sound against nonadaptive provers be boosted into stronger succinct arguments, when the workload is a large set of precommitted numerical statements? Specifically, is this possible for an aggregate of \(10^6\) statements fixed before setup, with succinctness depending only polylogarithmically on total execution length, and what limitations remain for later adaptive requests?
status: Removing adaptive soundness from the boosting premise is an explicit open question of Cheng and Goyal (2025, *Boosting SNARKs and Rate-1 Barrier in Arguments of Knowledge*), and no resolution is known.
solved_when: A boosting construction (or a refutation) is given for aggregates of \(10^6\) pre-set statements achieving polylogarithmic dependence on total execution length from a nonadaptively sound, mildly succinct starting proof, together with a characterization of what breaks when requests become adaptive after setup.
why: Scheduled training and evaluation campaigns naturally fix their computational workload in advance, so they may be verifiable under weaker starting assumptions than fully adaptive workloads require.
key_works: Jiaqi Cheng, Rishab Goyal (2025), [*Boosting SNARKs and Rate-1 Barrier in Arguments of Knowledge*](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.56).

title: Certificate-size barriers for universally quantified numerical claims
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Which restricted classes of neural-network safety claims — statements quantified over all inputs — admit polynomial-size witnesses checkable by ordinary NP SNARKs? In particular, classify certificate sizes as a function of circuit size \(S\), precision \(b\), and the number \(k\) of unstable ReLUs, and determine whether certificates of size \(2^{o(k)}\operatorname{poly}(S,b)\) are possible under the stated assumptions.
status: Alsmann, Lange and Sälzer establish complexity results for quantized verification formulations; these do not make every universal safety property cheaply certifiable. See Eric Alsmann, Martin Lange, Marco Sälzer (2026), *The Complexity of Verifying Feedforward Neural Networks in Quantised Settings*, arXiv:2605.29537.
solved_when: A classification exists identifying the restricted neural safety claims with polynomial-size witnesses for ordinary NP SNARKs, together with certificate bounds in terms of \(S\), \(b\), and \(k\) — specifically settling whether \(2^{o(k)}\operatorname{poly}(S,b)\)-size certificates are achievable under the stated assumptions.
why: Compressing a supplied certificate does not make finding a certificate for a universal property easy, so these size barriers delineate what ordinary NP SNARKs can ever certify about universally quantified numerical claims.
key_works: Eric Alsmann, Martin Lange, Marco Sälzer (2026), [*The Complexity of Verifying Feedforward Neural Networks in Quantised Settings*, arXiv:2605.29537](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29537).

title: Conservative offline-RL penalty and sampling-error certificates
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Can CQL's sampled data-action and log-partition terms be given a statistical certificate for the error introduced by Monte Carlo sampling itself? Formally, after fixing Q and the proposal densities under a declared normalized reference measure, use fresh conditional samples with bounded-Q/domination assumptions to certify per-update 99% coverage of the sampling error at most 0.01, while budgeting simultaneous adaptive coverage separately.
status: CQL (Kumar, Zhou, Tucker, Levine, 2020, arXiv:2006.04779) supplies conservative-value theory and practical sampled objectives, but a proof of the sampled arithmetic alone does not establish its population lower-bound claims.
solved_when: A proof exists that, for fixed Q and proposal densities, fresh conditional samples under bounded-Q/domination assumptions yield per-update coverage at 99% of the sampling error with a bound of 0.01, together with a separate treatment of simultaneous adaptive coverage.
why: Numerical correctness and statistical validity must both hold for a conservative-value certificate to be meaningful — a proof of the sampled arithmetic alone does not establish CQL's population lower-bound claims.
key_works: Aviral Kumar, Aurick Zhou, George Tucker, Sergey Levine (2020), [*Conservative Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning*, arXiv:2006.04779](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.04779).

title: Cross-tokenizer sorted-probability distillation certificates
subfield: Distillation and alternative preference objectives
open: Can we build a verifiable computation certificate for cross-tokenizer distillation that covers the entire ULD surrogate — the padded, independently sorted probability vectors, the tokenizer outputs, the position pairing, the tie rules, and the final student gradient — while keeping token identities and ranks hidden? Formally, the target is 32K and 128K vocabularies over 2K paired positions, with only \(O(V\log V)\) auxiliary work in the proof system.
status: ULD (Nicolas Boizard, Kevin El Haddad, Céline Hudelot, Pierre Colombo (2025 revision), [*Towards Cross-Tokenizer Distillation: the Universal Logit Distillation Loss for LLMs*, arXiv:2402.12030](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.12030v3)) provides a cross-tokenizer sorted-probability surrogate, but certifying that surrogate does not establish semantic equivalence of the vocabularies.
solved_when: A certificate exists that proves correctness of ULD's padded, independently sorted probability vectors, tokenizer outputs, position pairing, tie rules, and student gradient for 32K/128K vocabularies over 2K paired positions, within an \(O(V\log V)\) auxiliary-work budget and with hidden token identities and ranks.
why: Without such a certificate, tokenization and alignment choices sit outside the proved distillation loss, so the surrogate's fidelity to the actual computation is unverified.
key_works: Nicolas Boizard, Kevin El Haddad, Céline Hudelot, Pierre Colombo (2025 revision), [*Towards Cross-Tokenizer Distillation: the Universal Logit Distillation Loss for LLMs*, arXiv:2402.12030](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.12030v3).

title: Contrastive distillation with a private authenticated negative bank
subfield: Distillation and alternative preference objectives
open: Can a contrastive distillation pipeline be bound to its full loss and gradient computation, so that the positive teacher–student pairs, the negative sampling, the feature-bank version, and the projection-head state are all covered by a single verifiable proof? Formally, the goal is a private authenticated negative bank at the scale of a \(10^6\)-example bank with 16K negatives per update, where proof work grows only with the entries actually accessed and sample identities remain hidden.
status: Contrastive Representation Distillation (Tian, Krishnan, Isola, 2020, arXiv:1910.10699) supplies the representation-transfer objective, but private authenticated bank access and complete update proofs each remain separate open obligations.
solved_when: A construction exists that binds the complete loss and gradient to the positive pair selection, negative sampling, feature-bank state, and projection-head state, handling a \(10^6\)-example bank with 16K negatives per update, with proof cost proportional to accessed entries and without revealing sample identities.
why: Without authenticated bank access, forged or stale negatives can silently change the training objective while all supplied features still pass arithmetic checks — the verifier confirms the math but not the objective.
key_works: Yonglong Tian, Dilip Krishnan, Phillip Isola (2020), [*Contrastive Representation Distillation*, arXiv:1910.10699](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10699).

title: IPO squared-margin stationary-point certificates
subfield: Distillation and alternative preference objectives
open: Can we formally certify that the IPO training objective behaves as intended around its optimum — specifically, that its squared log-ratio-margin objective and update direction are correct on both sides of the finite target margin, so that the isolated scalar optimum is preserved under numerical perturbation?
status: The ΨPO/IPO analysis of Azar et al. (2024) ([arXiv:2310.12036](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.12036)) supplies the squared-margin objective, but a DPO score certificate does not establish IPO’s stationary point or gradient sign.
solved_when: A proof shows that the derived precision conditions perturb the isolated scalar optimum by at most \(10^{-3}\), and that private updates are certified for batches of 1,024 preference pairs.
why: Numerical approximation can shift the equilibrium of the intended preference objective, so without these certificates IPO training may converge to a stationary point of a different objective than the one designed.
key_works: Mohammad Gheshlaghi Azar et al. (2024), [*A General Theoretical Paradigm to Understand Learning from Human Preferences*, arXiv:2310.12036](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.12036).

title: KTO surrogate-reference and unpaired-label proofs
subfield: Distillation and alternative preference objectives
open: Can an LLM inference serve a succinct proof that its KTO training step was carried out honestly, with all of KTO's distinctive mechanics — desirable/undesirable example weighting, cyclically mismatched microbatches, clamped reference values, and stopped gradients through the reference — proved rather than assumed? The proof should additionally keep both the labels and the reference model private.
status: KTO's September 2026 revision explicitly describes a biased KL surrogate and a stopped-gradient reference, so any certificate must be stated in terms of that surrogate rather than true KL. Key work: Kawin Ethayarajh, Winnie Xu, Niklas Muennighoff, Dan Jurafsky, Douwe Kiela (2024; revised 2026), [*KTO: Model Alignment as Prospect Theoretic Optimization*, arXiv:2402.01306v5](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.01306v5).
solved_when: A verifiable proof covers the KTO step over 4,096 unpaired examples, includes all four mechanics above, adds less than 10% overhead beyond the likelihood/backward proofs, and preserves privacy of labels and the reference; the certificate must name KTO's biased KL surrogate rather than claiming true KL.
why: The reference-estimation shortcut and stopped-gradient handling are real parts of the computation, and without proving them the certificate would silently misrepresent what was actually computed.
key_works: Kawin Ethayarajh, Winnie Xu, Niklas Muennighoff, Dan Jurafsky, Douwe Kiela (2024; revised 2026), [*KTO: Model Alignment as Prospect Theoretic Optimization*, arXiv:2402.01306v5](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.01306v5).

title: ORPO odds-ratio numerics and joint-objective proofs
subfield: Distillation and alternative preference objectives
open: Can the two components of ORPO's objective — the chosen-response likelihood term and the odds-ratio preference term — be given a unified numerical treatment, with a single length-normalization convention carried consistently through one backward pass, and with certified numerics near the probability boundaries?
status: ORPO defines a reference-free joint preference objective (Hong, Lee, and Thorne, 2024, arXiv:2403.07691); stable numerical certification of its terms and the complete private update remain proposed extensions, not yet established.
solved_when: For all probabilities in \([2^{-24}, 1-2^{-24}]\), a gradient-error envelope is certified for both terms under the unified convention and backward pass, and it is validated against \(10^6\) adversarial boundary cases.
why: Near-boundary logarithms can shift gradients or invalidate naive lookup approximations, so without certified evaluation the reported preference optimization may not reflect the objective actually being optimized.
key_works: Jiwoo Hong, Noah Lee, James Thorne (2024), [*ORPO: Monolithic Preference Optimization without Reference Model*, arXiv:2403.07691](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07691).

title: Permutation-alignment optimality before private model merging
subfield: Model merging, continual learning, and episodic meta-training
open: Can we certify, before merging neural networks privately, that the hidden-unit permutations used for alignment are both architecture-respecting and provably optimal for each declared linear-assignment subproblem at width 16,384, while keeping the auxiliary cost at \(O(d^2)\)? Exact function preservation would require suitable fixed-point reductions, and general floating-point implementations would need a proved reordering-error bound.
status: Git Re-Basin (Samuel K. Ainsworth, Jonathan Hayase, Siddhartha Srinivasa, 2023, arXiv:2209.04836) supplies permutation-based alignment and merging. Global optimality over all layers, and exact GPU numerical equivalence, do not follow from that construction.
solved_when: For each declared linear-assignment subproblem at width 16,384, a certificate confirms the architecture-respecting permutation is optimal, the total auxiliary computation is \(O(d^2)\), and either exact function preservation via fixed-point reductions is established or a proved bound on floating-point reordering error is supplied.
why: Without such certificates, an algebraic symmetry used in merging may fail to preserve the deployed program's numerical output, so merged models cannot be trusted to compute the same function.
key_works: Samuel K. Ainsworth, Jonathan Hayase, Siddhartha Srinivasa (2023), [*Git Re-Basin: Merging Models modulo Permutation Symmetries*, arXiv:2209.04836](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04836).

title: DoReMi proxy-to-training mixture certificates
subfield: Data curricula and alternative optimizer state
open: Can a language-model training run prove that its data mixture was honestly derived from proxy-model losses — i.e., certified computation of reference losses, clipped excess losses, exponentiated reweighting, smoothing, and averaged domain weights, with the main model's sampling bound to those weights?
status: DoReMi (Sang Michael Xie et al. (2023), [arXiv:2305.10429](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10429)) uses a proxy model to choose a larger model's data mixture; making its two-stage pipeline privately provable remains an open engineering target.
solved_when: A verifiable certificate covers the full DoReMi pipeline at the target scale: 64 domains, \(10^6\) proxy updates, and \(10^9\) main-training tokens, all with under 5% auxiliary overhead.
why: A certified training run can still use an unauthorized data mixture unless the derivation of the mixture itself is included in what is proven.
key_works: Sang Michael Xie et al. (2023), [*DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining*, arXiv:2305.10429](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10429).

title: SAM perturbation, restore, and second-gradient binding
subfield: Data curricula and alternative optimizer state
open: Can the full Sharpness-Aware Minimization step — the first gradient, the normalized perturbation, the gradient at the perturbed weights, the restoration, and the final update — be proved correct under declared batch and randomness conventions, including stopped gradients and normalization buffers? The target is a machine-checkable certificate that scales to models with 1B parameters while costing at most 1.25× the proof cost of two ordinary gradient steps.
status: SAM approximates a neighborhood min–max objective through a second pass, so any certificate must cover that approximation rather than claim exact inner maximization. No such certificate currently exists. The underlying method is due to Pierre Foret, Ariel Kleiner, Hossein Mobahi, and Behnam Neyshabur (2021), *Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Efficiently Improving Generalization* (arXiv:2010.01412); related directions include transactional state restoration, certified bilevel approximations, and numerical perturbation analysis.
solved_when: A verified implementation of the complete SAM update exists, with a certificate covering the first gradient, normalized perturbation, gradient at perturbed weights, restoration, and final update (with stopped gradients and normalization buffers handled), certified at the 1B-parameter scale within the stated 1.25× budget relative to two ordinary gradient steps, under the declared batch/randomness conventions.
why: A second gradient is meaningful only when it is bound to the correct perturbed state; without verified restoration, the SAM certificate would not correspond to the computation actually performed.
key_works: Pierre Foret, Ariel Kleiner, Hossein Mobahi, Behnam Neyshabur (2021), [*Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Efficiently Improving Generalization*, arXiv:2010.01412](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01412).

title: Long-form ASR seek, silence, and fallback integrity
subfield: Multimodal input, alignment, and output proofs
open: Can a proof system certify not just the neural calls of a long-form transcription but the orchestration around them — window overlaps, seek offsets, silence skipping, temperature fallbacks, and prior-text conditioning? Formally, for a 30-minute recording, prove exact accounting of processed versus skipped audio intervals so that no source material is silently dropped.
status: Whisper's reference transcriber implements orchestration logic beyond the encoder-decoder network, and faithfully executing that orchestration is distinct from the semantic correctness of recognition itself; no proof system currently covers it.
solved_when: A proof certifies faithful execution of the full transcriber pipeline (overlapping windows, seek offsets, silence skipping, temperature fallbacks, prior-text conditioning) on 30-minute recordings, with exact processed/skipped interval accounting and at most twice the witness memory required for one window.
why: Without orchestration proofs, a transcript can omit source intervals while every executed neural call remains individually valid, so the transcript no longer attests to what was actually said.
key_works: Alec Radford et al. (2022), [*Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04356); OpenAI Whisper contributors, [*transcribe.py*](https://github.com/openai/whisper/blob/main/whisper/transcribe.py).

title: Inpainting masks and forward-resampling trajectory proofs
subfield: Diffusion, flow, and iterative-generation proofs
open: Can we prove the full editing trajectory of masked diffusion inpainting — that mask-conditioned merges, the noise applied to known regions, reverse updates, and forward-resampling jumps all occurred as committed? A complete trajectory certificate would verify the entire sampling path rather than selected layers or merely the factual authenticity of the generated content.
status: RePaint establishes diffusion inpainting with resampling (Andreas Lugmayr et al. (2022), *RePaint: Inpainting using Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models*, arXiv:2201.09865). No complete trajectory certificate currently exists; such a certificate is distinct from selected-layer proofs or factual authenticity of generated content.
solved_when: A trajectory certificate exists covering mask-conditioned merges, known-region noise, reverse updates, and forward-resampling jumps, demonstrated across 100 masks on \(512^2\) images, with declared final-region preservation, complete jump coverage, and less than 10% schedule/mask overhead.
why: Both the edited regions and the preserved source evidence in an inpainted image must demonstrably follow the committed editing policy, so a verifier can trust not just the output but the process that produced it.
key_works: Andreas Lugmayr et al. (2022), [*RePaint: Inpainting using Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models*, arXiv:2201.09865](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.09865).

title: Denoiser feature-cache policy and distortion certificates
subfield: Diffusion, flow, and iterative-generation proofs
open: Can we give a proof-backed policy for when a diffusion denoiser should refresh its deep features versus reuse cached ones, so that accelerated generation is both verifiable and honestly measured? Formally, prove the feature refresh/reuse decisions, originating latents and timesteps, branch identity, and substitution policy of the cached execution trace.
status: DeepCache (Ma, Fang, and Wang, 2023, arXiv:2312.00858) reuses features across denoising stages as an inference acceleration, but it is an approximation: a valid cached trace is not automatically an exact uncached-model result, so reuse decisions currently carry no proof or certified quality guarantee.
solved_when: On 50-step generation, the scheme achieves 2× less proving work, while separately certifying a preregistered quality comparison over 10,000 prompt/seed pairs.
why: Approximate temporal reuse of denoiser features needs both execution evidence that the cache was followed as claimed and an honest quality measurement showing what the approximation costs.
key_works: Xinyin Ma, Gongfan Fang, Xinchao Wang (2023), [*DeepCache: Accelerating Diffusion Models for Free*, arXiv:2312.00858](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00858).

title: Continuous-flow likelihood-estimator certificates
subfield: Diffusion, flow, and iterative-generation proofs
open: Can a continuous normalizing flow's reported likelihood be certified by a proof that tracks the full computational pipeline — state trajectories, Hutchinson probes, Jacobian-vector products, quadrature, and log-density accumulation — rather than merely certifying sample generation? Concretely, for 1,024-dimensional densities the certificate should cost less than 3× the sample-generation proof time and yield separate certified bounds on integration error and estimator uncertainty.
status: FFJORD (Grathwohl et al., 2018, arXiv:1810.01367) computes continuous-flow densities via stochastic trace estimation (Hutchinson probes), but proving that estimator does not make the resulting likelihood exact. Flow matching (Lipman et al., 2022, arXiv:2210.02747) is a related continuous-flow framework; no existing work certifies the likelihood pipeline end to end.
solved_when: A proof system exists that, for 1,024-dimensional densities, certifies likelihood estimates produced via stochastic trace estimation in under 3× the sample-generation proof time, with distinct certified bounds for integration error and for estimator uncertainty.
why: A sample-generation proof does not authenticate an attached likelihood or uncertainty score, so downstream users of flow models currently have no way to trust reported densities; a certificate would close that gap.
key_works: Will Grathwohl et al. (2018), [*FFJORD: Free-form Continuous Dynamics for Scalable Reversible Generative Models*, arXiv:1810.01367](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.01367); Yaron Lipman et al. (2022), [*Flow Matching for Generative Modeling*, arXiv:2210.02747](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02747).

title: Query-rewrite and hypothetical-document derivation chains
subfield: Structured, learned, and distributed retrieval proofs
open: Can a retrieval-augmented pipeline prove it answered faithfully — that every rewritten query and hypothetical document was derived from the user's actual question, that every claimed expansion and retrieval round really ran, and that the merged context is the honest union of their results — without the proof dominating the pipeline's cost?
status: Query transformation before retrieval is standard practice: HyDE embeds hypothetical answer documents as search probes (Gao et al. 2022), and Rewrite-Retrieve-Read rewrites queries before retrieval (Ma et al. 2023). Verifiable-execution schemes prove that a committed computation ran, but none prove derivation integrity (each rewrite came from the committed model on the real query), branching completeness (no expansion or round dropped or substituted), or union-rule correctness for these pipelines.
solved_when: A proof system (ZK circuit or equivalent) tracing the full chain — query → rewrites/hypothetical documents → embeddings → retriever calls → result union, including expansion counts and randomness — that (a) proves each rewrite was derived by the committed model from the input query, (b) detects a dropped or substituted branch, and (c) at the reference workload of 8 expansions × 4 retrieval rounds adds less than 10% linkage overhead.
why: A pipeline can drop or substitute retrieval branches — silently censoring what the model is allowed to see — while every executed step still verifies. A practical proof would make "the model saw the whole retrieval" a checkable claim, which is what audited or adversarial RAG needs.
key_works: Luyu Gao et al. (2022), [*Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels*, arXiv:2212.10496](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10496); Xinbei Ma et al. (2023), [*Query Rewriting for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models*, arXiv:2305.14283](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14283).

title: Sampled-neighborhood GNN inference with complete adjacency access
subfield: Geometric, implicit, and dynamically parameterized architectures
open: Can a GraphSAGE-style inference over a large graph be proved in zero knowledge when the prover only samples neighborhoods, even though the full adjacency list is available to the verifier? Concretely, this demands sampling without replacement, authenticated adjacency and features, correct normalization, and complete aggregation over the selected neighbors — while hiding which vertices were never visited.
status: zkGCN (Ding et al., 2026) supplies R1CS-based zero-knowledge proofs of GCN inference with graph-classification experiments, but large private-graph sampling and integrity of adjacency access lie beyond its published scope.
solved_when: A verifiable proof system handles graphs with \(10^8\) edges and sampled subgraphs up to \(10^5\) vertices, achieving subgraph-proportional work and evidence below 1 MB, while concealing unvisited neighbors.
why: Biased neighborhood selection can silently change a model's predictions while all aggregation arithmetic remains correct, so verifying the math alone is not enough — the sampling itself must be proved faithful.
key_works: William L. Hamilton, Rex Ying, Jure Leskovec (2017), [*Inductive Representation Learning on Large Graphs*, arXiv:1706.02216](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02216); Hongfa Ding et al. (2026), [*ZkGCN: Zero-Knowledge Based Verifiable Inference for Graph Convolutional Networks*](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-95-8408-6_20).

title: Cross-verifier differential acceptance corpus
subfield: Implementation security of numerical proof services
open: Can the numerical proof-service ecosystem be stress-tested for cross-verifier portability with a large public differential corpus? The goal is to release one million valid and malformed proof instances, spanning six implementations of the same protocol and parameters across three processor architectures, and then classify and minimize every acceptance disagreement while preserving the public statement, tensor dimensions, and numerical mode.
status: The 2026 ZKP security-tool study evaluates six tools on 70 real bugs, principally circuit-analysis coverage; a cross-verifier acceptance corpus is a different data deliverable. See Arman Kolozyan, Tom Sorger, Alexander Hicks, Stefanos Chaliasos (2026), [ZKP Security Tools and Verification: Coverage, Effectiveness, Adoption, and Challenges, arXiv:2607.23752](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23752).
solved_when: A corpus of one million valid and malformed proof instances covering six implementations on three processor architectures is released, and every acceptance disagreement between the implementations is classified and minimized with the public statement, tensor dimensions, and numerical mode preserved.
why: Portability and parsing disagreements can make the same AI receipt valid to one service and invalid to another, undermining the reliability of verification across providers.
key_works: Arman Kolozyan, Tom Sorger, Alexander Hicks, Stefanos Chaliasos (2026), [*ZKP Security Tools and Verification: Coverage, Effectiveness, Adoption, and Challenges*, arXiv:2607.23752](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23752).

title: Incremental security revalidation after upgrades
subfield: Implementation security of numerical proof services
open: Can a verified proof stack survive routine compiler and dependency upgrades while keeping most of its assurance intact — detecting exactly which assumptions and obligations changed, rather than re-proving everything or silently breaking? Concretely, can maintenance tooling carry a proof stack through 100 successive upgrades, retaining at least 90% of unaffected proof artifacts and cutting median manual revalidation below 10% of a fresh verification, without papering over failures with unproved axioms?
status: Current studies document the friction this problem targets: the Rust-to-Lean pipeline work (Natalia Klaus et al., 2026, [A Rust-to-Lean Verification Pipeline with AI Provers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30106)) reports toolchain drift and extraction friction, and the ZKP-tool study (Arman Kolozyan et al., 2026, [ZKP Security Tools and Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23752)) reports integration gaps. A longitudinal proof-maintenance benchmark remains the proposed deliverable.
solved_when: A longitudinal proof-maintenance benchmark demonstrates a proof stack maintained through 100 compiler/dependency upgrades with explicit detection of changed assumptions and obligations, retention of at least 90% of unaffected proof artifacts, median manual revalidation under 10% of a fresh verification, and no use of unproved axioms to bypass failures.
why: Assurance that evaporates on the next dependency bump is of little use; provers and their toolchains evolve rapidly, so verified components are only deployable in practice if their guarantees survive routine upgrades.
key_works: Natalia Klaus et al. (2026), [*A Rust-to-Lean Verification Pipeline with AI Provers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30106); Arman Kolozyan et al. (2026), [*ZKP Security Tools and Verification*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23752).
